t: CourseForge is a self-hosted web application that uses AI to design, write and publish complete courses into a BookStack knowledge base. You describe what should be taught, to whom and up to which level, in one line. CourseForge turns that into a book with chapters and pages, writes the teaching content of every page, attaches tags and flashcards, and pushes the result into one or more BookStack wikis over their REST API. text Copy"Vue.js – complete course from beginner to professional; IDE: PhpStorm" │ ├─ AI designs the outline 20 chapters, 140 pages, a scope under each ├─ AI writes each page in the background, or at half price in a batch queue ├─ you steer what goes in per course, chapter or page └─ CourseForge publishes it into BookStack - one wiki or several, links and all You can do all of that in a browser, or from an AI client - Claude Code, the Claude desktop app, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, VS Code or Gemini CLI - which connects over the Model Context Protocol and can do everything the browser can.

The four stages of a course. A profile supplies the AI; a connected client can take over any step. The brief. A course starts as one sentence: the subject, the reader and how far the course should go. "Machine learning with Python, from a first linear model to a served pipeline, for developers who already write Python." The outline. The AI designs chapters and pages from the brief, and under every page one line - the page's scope - naming what that page and no other page teaches. The outline is Markdown: read it, edit it, ask the AI to revise it, then Apply it. See The outline. The pages. Every page is written from a brief that carries the course map, its own chapter, the content details that apply to it and the headings of the pages already written beside it. You can write pages one at a time while you watch, hand the whole course to a background run, or send it to the provider's batch queue at about half price. See Writing pages and Runs. Publishing. CourseForge creates the book in BookStack, puts it on a shelf, creates or updates every chapter and page with its tags, and turns cross-reference markers into real links. Pushing again only sends what changed. See Publishing.

Pages that do not repeat each other. A page is written in a request of its own, so it only knows about the rest of the course what its prompt tells it. CourseForge tells it what every other page owns, through the scopes, so the page on ref() leaves watch() to the page that teaches it and links there instead. How that works. A prompt a third the size, mostly cached. The shared part of every page prompt is byte-identical from page to page and is marked for each provider's prompt cache. On a course of 20 chapters × 7 pages, a page prompt went from about 139,000 characters to 47,000, and a live run on Anthropic is billed for roughly a tenth of the input it used to be. Nothing hidden. Every instruction the AI receives is one of 48 documented, editable prompt slots. An administrator can change them for the whole installation; anybody can override them for their own profile. See The prompt library. Made for a web host. It is PHP 8.1+ with SQLite and no dependencies to install. Long jobs survive a closed browser tab, a crashed worker or a host time limit, because work is written down before it starts and every page is stored the moment it is finished. Your provider, your price. CourseForge talks to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini and OpenRouter natively, to sixteen OpenAI-compatible gateways through presets, and to any other endpoint you type in, including a model running on your own machine. See AI providers.

Word Meaning Course One book being written: its brief, outline, chapters, pages, tags and where it publishes. Courses are listed under Courses. Outline (Structure) The course as Markdown: the book title and description, numbered chapters with a goal each, numbered pages, and a scope under each page. Apply turns it into chapters and pages. Scope The one line under a page in the outline that names what that page alone teaches. Every page is written knowing every other page's scope. Profile A reusable bundle of AI accounts, BookStack instances, models, course language, content defaults and prompt overrides. A course is written with one profile. AI account One connection to a model provider: a type (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, a preset or a custom endpoint), a key and an address. Model slots A profile has two: the model that designs the outline and the model that writes the pages. They can use different accounts. Content details The elements a page is made of (summary, exercises, diagrams, formulas, Anki cards…) and the values that size them (minimum length, exercises per page…). Inherited from installation to profile to course to chapter to page. Run A batch of pages the server writes for you, in the background from cron or through a provider's batch queue. A run survives the tab, the session and a restart. Destination A BookStack instance a course publishes into, with its own shelf and its own book. A course may have several. Look A BookStackDev configuration that decides how a wiki renders code, diagrams and formulas, loaded by one line in BookStack's custom head.

A web host with PHP 8.1 or newer (8.4 or 8.5 recommended) and the cURL, PDO SQLite, mbstring, json and session extensions. A BookStack instance with an API token, if you want to publish. You can write a whole course without one. An AI provider account, or an MCP client such as Claude Code to do the writing. You need at least one of them. Optionally, a way to call a URL once a minute (any hosting control panel's cron), which is what lets runs and publishing carry on with the browser closed. The full list is on Installation.

Trying it out? Follow the Quick start: from a fresh install to a published course. Setting up a server? Read Installation, then Security and The scheduler. Using Claude Code or the Claude app? Go to Connect an AI client. Watching the bill? Read Runs and Tokens and caching.

CourseForge is a folder of files. There is no installer, no package manager and no build step: copy the folder to a PHP host, make one directory writable and open it in a browser. Everything else - AI accounts, BookStack instances, the scheduler, the security policy, the prompt library - is set from inside the application.

Needed Notes PHP 8.1 or newer 8.4 or 8.5 is faster and is what CourseForge is developed on. An 8.0 interpreter cannot even parse the code and serves a blank page. Extensions cURL, PDO SQLite, mbstring, json, session All five ship with almost every PHP build. Web server anything that serves files and runs PHP Apache and LiteSpeed read the shipped .htaccess. nginx, Caddy and IIS need a few lines of configuration. Network outbound HTTPS To your AI provider and your BookStack instance. Browser import-map support Chrome/Edge 89+, Firefox 108+, Safari 16.4+. Diagrams in the preview need Safari 17.4+. Optional, only for the features that use them: A scheduler that calls a URL once a minute (a control-panel cron) or a real crontab. Without it, pages are still written, but only while a browser tab is open: no background runs, no batch collection, no unattended updates. See The scheduler. ext-zip, to install updates from GitHub. proc_open enabled, so that an update can test the new release's database migration in a child process before accepting it. Where it is disabled, that one check is skipped and the update log says so. NoteThere is no Composer, no npm and no compile step - in development or in production. The browser loads Vue and every other library as ES modules through an import map, so deploying is copying files.

Download a release. Take the latest zip from GitHub Releases ("Source code (zip)"), or clone the repository: bash Copygit clone https://github.com/ZcarecroW/CourseForge.git courseforge Copy the files to your web root, or to a subdirectory of it. The document root is the folder holding index.html and api/. A subdirectory works as it is: every URL is relative. Make data/ writable by the user PHP runs as. The SQLite database (data/app.sqlite, created and migrated on first open), the settings this installation changes, the staged updates and the backups all live there. bash Copychmod 775 data # or chown it to the PHP user Open the address in a browser. CourseForge writes a one-time code to INVITE-CODE.txt next to index.html - or into data/ if the install root is not writable - and shows the setup screen, which names the path it used. Create the first administrator. Copy the code out of that file into the setup screen, with a user name and a password of at least ten characters. That account is the first administrator and is signed in straight away. The file is deleted the moment it is used. TipIf you have a shell, php tools/diagnose.php checks the installation and prints what is wrong: a read-only data directory, a missing extension, a scheduler that has never ticked. The same rows are on Administration › Settings › Diagnostics for hosts with no shell.

h: Why a code in a file?
t: A fresh installation is a web address with no accounts and a form that creates the first one. Whoever reaches that form first would own the installation, and bots scanning for new hosts are faster than people. The code lives only in a file on the server, so only somebody who could put files on the server can use it. It is six groups of four characters from an alphabet without look-alikes (no I, O, 0 or 1); case, spaces and hyphens are ignored when you type it. Once any account exists, the setup route refuses to create anything, for good. If the file is lost before it is used, delete the open row from the invites table and reload: a fresh code is written. More on accounts in Accounts and roles.

A guided tour starts by itself and walks through every screen. Then do these three things, in this order. Pass the security check. Open Administration › Security. CourseForge asks the server for its own private files over HTTP and reports which came back. Until every one is refused, all fields that would store an API key or a token stay locked, with a red mark. On Apache with the shipped .htaccess this passes by itself; on nginx, Caddy or IIS paste the configuration block the screen gives you. See Security. Set up the scheduler. Open Administration › Settings › Scheduler, generate a cron token and paste the URL it gives you into your host's cron, every minute. See The scheduler. Create a profile with an AI account and, if you publish, a BookStack instance. Then create your first course. The Quick start walks through it.

Shared hosting usually hands out limits chosen for a blog: sixty seconds of execution, a socket timeout shorter than a model takes to write a page, 128 MB of memory. Administration › Settings › Set up PHP measures what the host gives and writes a .user.ini that raises exactly the limits that are too low. It runs by itself the first time an administrator opens the application. Every number is a floor, never a value: a host that gives 768 MB keeps 768 MB; a host that gives 128 MB is asked for 256 MB. Nothing is ever lowered. Directive Floor Why memory_limit 256M A course tree, its pages and an update archive are held at once. max_execution_time 300 Writing a page, publishing a book and installing an update all take longer than a minute. default_socket_timeout 300 A model can take minutes to answer; at sixty seconds the page is cut off and recorded as failed. max_input_time 300 How long PHP spends reading a request body. post_max_size 32M A finished page, its outline and its tags arrive in one request. upload_max_filesize 32M Restoring a backup means uploading the archive an update made. max_input_vars 5000 A course with hundreds of pages sends more fields than the default thousand. display_errors Off An error page that prints a file path tells a stranger where the database is. log_errors On What is not displayed still has to go somewhere. output_buffering Off A long answer held in a buffer is held in memory twice. .user.ini is read by the CGI, FastCGI and FPM SAPIs. h: Keep the data directory out of the web root
t: data/app.sqlite holds every password hash and, in plain text, every AI key and BookStack token the installation has been given. The shipped .htaccess denies it, and CourseForge rewrites data/.htaccess itself if it goes missing - but the arrangement that is safe on every server is a data directory that is not under the document root at all: Apache CopySetEnv COURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR /var/lib/courseforge nginx Copyfastcgi_param COURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR /var/lib/courseforge; Then only index.html, assets/, api/, cron.php and bs.php need to be public. config/ must stay readable by PHP but not by the web. The invite code goes into the data directory in this arrangement, since the install root is usually not writable.

h: Trying it on your own machine
t: PHP's built-in server is enough to evaluate CourseForge on a laptop: bash Copycd courseforge php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 -t . tools/router-dev.php Then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/. tools/router-dev.php reproduces the most important .htaccess rules, but not all of them: under php -S, config/defaults.json and INVITE-CODE.txt can be downloaded. That is fine on a laptop and not a way to serve CourseForge to anybody else. To keep the database away from the code while you try things, point the data directory elsewhere: bash CopyCOURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR=/tmp/cf-data php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 -t . tools/router-dev.php

This walk-through assumes CourseForge is installed and you are signed in as the first administrator (Installation). You will create a profile, a course and its outline, write the pages and publish the book. TipNo AI account? You can still follow along: design the outline and write the pages from Claude Code or another AI client instead, as described in Connect an AI client. Everything from step 4 on works the same.

A profile says who writes a course and where it goes. Open Profiles and click New profile. A profile has four tabs; for a first course you only need the first two. Profiles › Accounts: the wikis a course can publish into and the AI accounts that write it. Accounts. Under AI accounts, click Add and choose a type: Anthropic API, OpenAI, Google Gemini or OpenRouter: paste the API key. One of sixteen presets (Groq, DeepSeek, Together, Mistral, a local Ollama…): the address and quirks are filled in; local servers need no key. Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint: any address you type. Click Check this account to fetch the model list and prove the key works. Then, if you want to publish, add a BookStack instance on the left: its base URL and an API token id and secret (in BookStack: your profile › Access & security › API tokens; the user needs permission to create books, chapters and pages). NoteKey fields stay greyed out with a red mark until Administration › Security has passed. CourseForge refuses to store a secret in a database the web server might hand to anybody. See Security. Models & output. Pick which account and model designs the outline and which writes the pages. A strong model for the outline is worth it: it is one request. Set the course language and how many pages are written in parallel. Tick write these pages through the provider's batch queue if you want the whole course at about half price and can wait up to a day. Save. The other two tabs - Content defaults and Prompts - can wait. See Profiles.

Open Courses and click New course. Describe what should be taught, to whom and how far, in a full sentence. A good brief is specific: text CopyMachine learning with Python - from a first linear model to a served pipeline, for developers who already write Python but have never trained a model. Pick the profile you just made. You land in the course workspace, which has five tabs: Structure, Content, Details, Publish and Settings.

On the Structure tab, the AI panel is on the right. Click Design a new outline. One request later, the editor on the left holds the outline as Markdown, and the middle shows what Apply would make of it: the book title and tags, one box per chapter with its pages numbered, and each page's scope underneath. The Structure tab. The scope under each page names what that page, and no other page, teaches. Read it. This is the cheapest moment to change the course: Edit the Markdown directly: rename, reorder, add or delete pages, rewrite a scope. Request changes in the AI panel: "merge chapters 4 and 5, add a chapter on testing". The AI revises the outline and keeps every title you did not ask it to change. When it looks right, click Apply. Chapters and pages are created; nothing is written yet. The outline format is documented on The outline. TipIf some pages show no scope - an older outline, or pages you added by hand - click Plan missing scopes. One request plans them all, so every page knows what its neighbours cover.

The Details tab decides what every page of the course is made of: learning objectives, a summary, exercises, code examples, tables, callouts, Mermaid diagrams, formulas, Anki cards, cross references, web research - and how long a page should be. Each row inherits from the profile and the installation until you switch it on or off here. Details: elements on the left, values on the right. A green mark means this level decided; the arrow shows what it inherits. Chapters and pages can override the course in the Content tab's inspector. See Content details.

Open the Content tab. The outline is on the left with a status dot per page, the editor in the middle and the inspector on the right. The Content tab. A page in split mode: Markdown on the left, rendered as BookStack will show it on the right. At the bottom of the outline, choose what to write - Write all missing pages, Write the next N pages, Retry the failed pages or Rewrite everything - and start it: Choice What happens Close the tab? Write them here The browser writes N pages at a time and you watch each land. No Start run The server writes them in the background, from the scheduler. Yes Queue as a batch The provider's batch queue writes them within a day, at about half price. Yes Which buttons appear depends on the profile and on whether the scheduler is running. A run shows as a card with its own progress; it is still there tomorrow. Before a large run, the estimate tells you how many pages and roughly how many tokens are involved. See Runs.

Click a page to open it. The editor is a full Markdown editor (Ctrl+S saves); the preview renders code, diagrams and formulas the way BookStack will. To change a page by hand, edit it and save. To have the AI rewrite it with a correction, write the correction into the feedback box and click Rewrite this page: "the second example uses a deprecated API; use the current one". To give the AI facts it should treat as given for one page, use the context tab of the inspector. The page's scope is there too. See Writing pages.

Open the Publish tab. Click Add destination, pick the BookStack instance from your profile, load its shelves, pick one, and Save. Then click Publish everything. Publish. A push is a task the scheduler works through; the log is kept on the server. The push is a task: you can close the tab and it carries on (with the scheduler running). CourseForge creates the book, puts it on the shelf, creates every chapter and page with its tags, and resolves cross references into real links at the end. Publishing again later only sends what changed. See Publishing.

Make BookStack render code, diagrams and formulas properly: BookStackDev. Write courses from Claude Code or the Claude app: Connect an AI client. Invite colleagues: Accounts and roles. Tune what the AI is told: The prompt library.

CourseForge is a single-page application: one window, a sidebar on the left and the screen you are working on beside it. Courses: the sidebar holds the workspace and, for an administrator, the administration screens.

The Workspace group is what everybody uses: Entry What it is for Courses Every course you can see, with how far it has got, which profile writes it and how many wikis it publishes to. An administrator sees every account's courses, each marked with its owner. Tags The reusable tag library. See Tags. Profiles AI accounts, BookStack instances, models, language, content defaults and prompt overrides. See Profiles. BookStackDev Looks: how your wikis render code, diagrams and formulas. See BookStackDev. Connect Tokens for AI clients that connect over MCP. See Connect an AI client. An administrator also has an Administration group: Accounts, Settings, Prompts, Updates and Security. A normal account never sees it, and the server refuses those routes to it regardless. At the foot of the sidebar are the Guided tour button, the theme switch, your account and Sign out. The same glyph marks the same thing everywhere in the application: the book is always a course, the sliders are always a profile, the plug is always a connection.

Opening a course shows five tabs: Tab What happens there Structure The outline: design it with the AI, edit it, plan page scopes, apply it. The outline Content Write, generate, review and edit pages; start runs. Writing pages Details What every page is made of, and the research briefing. Content details Publish Where the course goes, pushing it there, and the publish log. Publishing Settings Name, course prompt, profile, AI tagging, course tags, punctuation and deleting the course. Leaving a screen with unsaved work - a page you edited, an outline you changed but did not apply, a destination list you did not save - asks first, whether you leave by the sidebar, the back arrow or by closing the browser tab.

The first time an account signs in, a tour starts by itself: the screen dims and one thing at a time is lit up, with a card explaining what it is for. It covers every screen and, for an administrator, every group of settings - forty-odd steps. A normal account gets a shorter tour without the administration screens. The guided tour lights up one section at a time. Skip it with Skip tour or Esc, step through it with the arrow keys, and open it again whenever you like with Guided tour above the theme switch. It is offered automatically only once per account.

Three choices at the foot of the sidebar: Light, Dark and Auto, which follows the operating system and keeps following it. CourseForge opens in the dark theme. The editor, the code highlighting and the diagrams follow the theme without reloading.

The account entry at the bottom of the sidebar is where you change your display name - the name shown against everything you create - and your password. A password needs at least ten characters and must differ from the old one. Your user name cannot be changed, by you or by an administrator: it is the key every row you own is filed under. A new name means a new account and a transfer. An account whose password was set by an administrator is asked to choose its own at first sign-in. Five failed sign-ins lock the address out for fifteen minutes (both numbers are settings).

Until Administration › Security has passed, every field that would store a secret is greyed out with a red mark, and an administrator sees a banner at the top of every screen explaining why. Click it to open the Security screen. See Security.

Keys Where Does Tab on a fresh page everywhere offers a skip link past the navigation Ctrl S Content tab saves the page Ctrl F any editor find Ctrl Z / Ctrl Y any editor undo / redo, per page Tab any editor indents Esc, ←, → the tour skip, back, next

Below 1024 px the sidebar collapses into a drawer behind the ☰ button. On the Content tab, the inspector becomes a slide-over below 1280 px, and the Structure tab's AI panel becomes a drawer behind the sparkle button.

A profile is the reusable part of a course: who writes it, with which models, in which language, in which house style, and which wikis it may publish into. Several courses can share one profile; changing the profile changes all of them, except where a course has decided otherwise. Open Profiles in the sidebar and click New profile. A profile has four tabs: Accounts, Models & output, Content defaults and Prompts. Accounts: BookStack instances on the left, AI accounts on the right. Each instance can wear a BookStackDev look.

Add one per wiki: a name, the base URL, and an API token id and secret. Create the token in BookStack under your profile › Access & security › API tokens, for a user allowed to create books, chapters, pages and shelves. It is worth adding more than one instance even for a single course - a staging wiki and the live one, say. A course chooses which of the profile's instances it publishes into, and it may choose several. See Publishing. Each instance card has a Look select: the BookStackDev configuration that wiki wears, which decides how it renders code, diagrams and formulas.

Add one or more. Every account has a type, and the fields change with it: Type What it needs OpenAI An OpenAI API key. The model picker is curated, because /v1/models mixes embeddings, audio and every fine-tune in with the chat models. Anthropic API An sk-ant- key. The native Messages API and the Message Batches queue. Google Gemini (beta) A Gemini API key. The native generateContent API - see the note about Google's key migration on AI providers. OpenRouter One key for every vendor OpenRouter fronts. Model ids carry a vendor prefix, as in anthropic/claude-opus-5. A preset A gateway that speaks /chat/completions: Groq, DeepSeek, Together, Fireworks, xAI, Mistral, Cerebras, DeepInfra, Nebius, Moonshot, Z.ai, a LiteLLM proxy, or the local servers Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and llama.cpp. The address and quirks are filled in; the local ones need no key. Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint Any base URL you type, with nothing assumed. CourseForge probes it for a model list and a batch queue without spending anything. Check this account proves an account works before a course depends on it: it fetches the model list, and for anything with a batch queue it records what that queue can do for this key - which is a different question from what the endpoint offers in general. See AI providers for what each type supports. NoteSecrets never travel back to the browser. A stored key shows as •••••••• stored; leaving the field empty on save keeps it. A stored key is only kept for the address it was stored against: change the base URL and the key has to be entered again, so a key can never be re

Slot What it does Advice Outline Designs and revises the course outline, and plans page scopes. One request per course. Use your strongest model. Pages Writes every page. Hundreds of requests. A good mid-range model is usually the right trade. Each slot has its own account, so the outline can come from Anthropic and the pages from a cheaper gateway. The model box is a fuzzy search; fetch list pulls the live list from the provider. You can always type a model id by hand. Each slot also has a temperature and a token ceiling. The ceiling caps the length of one answer; leave it at 0 for the provider's own maximum. The temperature does not apply to Claude: since 5.3 CourseForge speaks Anthropic API version 2026-10-21, which refuses sampling parameters on every model, so none is sent. OpenAI's reasoning models refuse it as well, and CourseForge leaves it out for them.

Under the page slot, write these pages through the provider's batch queue appends :batch to the model id. That is CourseForge's marker for bulk generation at about half price: a run started on this profile goes to the provider's queue and comes back within a day. It is offered on the page slot only, and it is disabled - with the reason underneath - when the account cannot queue. Where the provider publishes which models its queue accepts, they are listed with the chosen one highlighted. See Runs. Regenerating a single page from the editor always runs live, whatever the slot says.

Course language: what every course on this profile is written in. A fuzzy list, or type any language at all. Pages in parallel: how many pages the in-tab generator writes at once (default 2, up to 12). Background runs use the scheduler's worker count instead. Correct the punctuation of a generated page: sets quotation marks, apostrophes, dashes and spacing the way the course language does before a page is stored. On by default; see Punctuation.

What every course on this profile starts from: the same elements and values as a course's Details tab, one level up, in the same editor. Only deviations are stored, so a profile that decides nothing passes the installation's defaults straight through, and a course that never disagreed with its profile follows it when it changes. This is where a house style lives - learning objectives on, a minimum length of 2,500 words, a standing audience. See Content details.

Every prompt CourseForge sends, grouped and documented, each overridable for this profile only - on top of whatever an administrator has set for the whole installation. The profile layer wins. A profile override that is deliberately left empty sends nothing at all for that slot, which is how you switch a block of instructions off. See The prompt library.

Profiles are cheap; make one per purpose. Typical sets: House style - the production model, the live wiki, the content defaults your team agreed on. Drafts - a local model through Ollama for trying outlines out, with no publishing. Batch - the same as House style with the batch switch on, for large courses that can wait a day. A course switches profile on its Settings tab.

A profile cannot be deleted while a generation run is still open under it. A batch submitted with its credentials is collected with its credentials, and deleting the profile mid-run would leave that batch running - and billing - at the provider with nothing left here to collect it. Stop the run, or let it finish, and the profile can go. Courses that used a deleted profile go back to the installation defaults and need a new profile before they can generate.

Everything on this screen has a tool: create_profile, update_profile, add_ai_account, delete_ai_account, add_bookstack_instance, delete_bookstack_instance, set_model_slot, set_profile_details, set_profile_prompts, list_providers and more. Keys can be replaced over MCP but never read. See the MCP tool reference.

The Structure tab is where a course gets its shape. The outline is plain Markdown: a title, a description, numbered chapters with a goal each, numbered pages, and a one-line scope under every page. The AI writes the first version from the course brief; you read it, change it and Apply it. Left: the outline in an editor. Middle: what Apply would make of it, with every page's scope. Right: the AI panel.

The tab is a split view, like the Content tab's editor: Left: the outline in a Markdown editor, highlighted as Markdown with the {{Tag, Tag}} markers picked out. Middle: what Apply would make of it, parsed as you type: the book title and its tags, the description, one box per chapter with its pages numbered and their scopes underneath, and a count of what is new, moved and kept. A page the outline no longer names is listed underneath in red, because applying deletes it - with its text. Right: the AI panel (a drawer behind the sparkle button on narrow screens): the course prompt, Design a new outline, Request changes, and Page scopes. The two halves scroll together, passage for passage; the link button in the toolbar unlinks them, and edit and preview give either half the whole width.

Title indented under a chapter A page. A line indented deeper than a page The page's scope. {{Tag, Tag}} behind a title, or on the line below Tags for the book, chapter or page. See Tags. The parser is forgiving, because models drift: it also accepts bullets instead of numbers, 1) markers, bold titles and stray blank lines. A list item that reads like a sentence - long, with a full stop - is treated as description rather than as a page, so a descr

The scope is the most important line in the outline. It names what that page and no other page teaches: markdown Copy2. Reactivity Hold state that the page follows. 1. Reactive state with ref and reactive ref(); reactive(); when to use which; unwrapping in templates 2. Computed values and watchers computed(); caching; watch(); watchEffect() Every page is written knowing every other page's scope - the course map. So the page on ref sees that watch() belongs to the next page, and mentions that page instead of teaching watch() a second time. Scopes are how a course of a hundred independently written pages stays free of repetition. Where scopes come from: Designing an outline produces them: the outline prompt asks for scopes that divide the subject between the pages without overlap. That request is the one moment anything sees the whole course at once. Plan missing scopes in the AI panel fills them in, in one request for the whole course, for every page that has none - an outline from before 5.3, or pages you added by hand. The circular button next to it plans every page afresh. You can write or edit a scope like any other line of the outline, or in the Content tab's context inspector, where it sits above the page's extra context. The preview shows each scope under its page and counts the pages that have none. A page with no scope is still written - it is told to work out its share from its title and the course map - but planned scopes divide a subject far more cleanly. TipGood scopes are lists of concrete concepts separated by semicolons, not sentences: "computed(); caching; w

Design a new outline sends the course prompt (the brief, which you can edit in the panel or on the Settings tab) to the profile's outline model and puts the answer in the editor. Nothing is applied until you click Apply. Request changes asks the AI to revise the existing outline instead: "merge chapters 4 and 5", "add a chapter on testing before deployment", "make the pages shorter and more numerous". The AI is told to reproduce every title it does not change character for character, because titles are what keep written pages attached (below). If the course has web research switched on, the outline is designed from the stored research briefing, so a course about a library is built around its current version. See Research.

Apply parses the Markdown into chapters and pages, and matches them against what the course already has by title: A page whose title did not change keeps its content, its tags, its content details and its publishing record, wherever it moved to. A page with a new title is new. A page the outline no longer names is deleted with its text. So a rename detaches a page's content deliberately. The preview shows the renamed page as new and the old one as removed, in red - that is the moment to notice. If you want to rename a written page and keep its text, rename it in the Content tab's chapter or page editor instead: that renames the row and rewrites the outline for you. If the outline cannot be parsed into at least one chapter, nothing is changed at all. An AI answer that is not an outline can never wipe a course. WarningOver MCP, apply_structure refuses to delete pages that already have text unless the client confirms it - and clients on the 2026-07-28 protocol revision are asked the question interactively. In the browser, the red list in the preview is your confirmation.

h: The outline and the published book
t: The book title and description go onto the BookStack book; chapter goals become chapter descriptions; tags become BookStack tags. Scopes are not published: they are instructions for the writer, not text for the reader.

Tool Does get_structure_brief The prompt CourseForge would send to design an outline, for a client to design it itself. preview_structure Parses an outline and reports what applying it would create, keep and delete. apply_structure Applies an outline. generate_structure Has the course's own model design or revise the outline. Spends credit. plan_page_scopes Plans the scope of every page that has none (all for every page). Spends credit. See the MCP tool reference.

The Content tab is where pages get written: by the AI in this tab while you watch, by a background run or a batch, or by hand. Three panes on a wide screen: Left: the outline with status dots and the generation controls. Middle: the editor in split mode. Right: the inspector. Left: the outline, with a status dot per page, a filter, a search box and the generation controls at the bottom. Middle: the editor: the page title, the Markdown body in edit, split or preview mode, a word count and a link to the published page. Right: the inspector - details, tags and context for whatever is selected. Below 1280 px it becomes a slide-over. Selecting a chapter instead of a page turns the middle pane into a chapter editor (title and goal) and points the inspector at the chapter.

Dot Status grey not written yet amber, pulsing being written right now blue written amber changed since it was last published green published and in sync red the last attempt failed - hover for the reason The filter above the outline narrows the list to Not written yet, Written, Changed since publish or Failed. A link icon marks pages that contain cross-reference markers (Auto links).

The panel at the bottom of the outline chooses what to write: Choice Writes Write all missing pages every page that has no text yet Write the next N pages the next N unwritten pages in reading order Retry the failed pages only the pages whose last attempt failed Rewrite everything every page, replacing what is there …and how: In this tab - the browser runs as many requests in parallel as the profile allows and you watch each page land. Pages already written are kept; Stop stops. It is a loop in the browser, so it stops when the tab closes. As a run - the server takes over, in the background from the scheduler, or through the provider's batch queue at about half price. The button offers whichever the course is set up for, with or write them now, in this tab underneath. A run shows as a card with its own progress and is still there tomorrow. Which to use, what each costs and how to stop one is on Runs. A page that belongs to a run cannot be started again - not by a second run, not by the in-tab generator, not by Rewrite this page. The database enforces it, so two browser tabs cannot both start the same course.

h: What the AI is told about a page
t: Every page is written from a brief that carries: the course map - every chapter, and every page with its title and scope, numbered chapter.page; its own chapter and the chapter's goal; its own place, scope and tags, and the pages either side of it; the section headings of the pages already written in its chapter, which is where plans drift; the resolved content details - which elements to include, how long, for whom; the course's research briefing, if it has one; the page's extra context, and on a rewrite your feedback. That is how a page knows what the others teach without reading them. The shared part is the same for every page and is cached by the provider. The full assembly order is on The prompt library; the reasoning and the measurements are on Tokens and caching.

The inspector's context tab holds two things the AI reads for this page only: Scope - what this page alone teaches. The same line as in the outline; editing it here rewrites the outline. Extra context - facts and instructions that outrank the model's own assumptions: "use the uv workflow, not pip", "the examples target PostgreSQL 18". Saved with the page and sent with every generation of it. To correct a page that is already written, type the correction into the feedback box and click Rewrite this page. The AI receives the existing text and your feedback and rewrites the page. Leaving the box empty writes the page from scratch. The inspector's details tab overrides the course's content details for this page; tags attaches tags to it.

The left half of the editor is a full CodeMirror editor, not a text box: Headings, emphasis, links, quotes, list markers and inline code are highlighted as you type; a fenced block is highlighted in its own language, for over a hundred languages. Two CourseForge markers are picked out, so a malformed one is visible before it is published: a cross reference (🔗 Exact Title) and an Anki cloze {{c1::hidden text}}. Ctrl+F finds, Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, Tab indents, brackets close themselves, long lines wrap. Undo history belongs to the page: switching pages cannot undo into the wrong one. Ctrl+S saves. Leaving with unsaved edits asks first.

The right half renders the page the way BookStack will: Code is highlighted with the grammars VS Code uses, in 232 languages, loaded one grammar at a time as they are needed. Every block has a header with its language and three controls: copy, line numbers and line wrapping (the last two apply everywhere and are remembered). Diagrams: a ```mermaid block is drawn as you type. A diagram that does not parse shows Mermaid's own error with the line and column, which is the point of having it here rather than discovering it after a publish. Formulas: \( … \) inline and $$ … $$ display maths are typeset with MathJax - the delimiters the prompts ask for and BookStack renders. A single $ is left alone, so prices stay prices. In split mode the two halves scroll together, matched block by block rather than by percentage, so a tall diagram does not throw the alignment off. The ⇅ button turns linking off and on; whichever half you touched last leads.

h: Code blocks with no language, or the wrong one
t: AIs write many fenced blocks and do not always label them. When a fence names no language, says text, or names a language that clearly does not match its contents, CourseForge reads the block and works the language out - in the preview and the editor alike. It is built to decline rather than guess. Each language is recognised by things that are hard to write by accident (defmodule, #include <stdio.h>, let mut, { get; set; }), and a guess is only used when one language is well clear of every other. Program output, a directory tree or a line of prose stays plain. The fence says What it takes to override it nothing a clear winner text, plain, none a strong winner - the author may have meant it a language an emphatic one, for a language the detector can assess A language that was worked out rather than read off the fence is marked auto in the block header; hover it to see what happened.
The word count under the editor is the same count get_page and the course list report, over the Markdown as stored. Chinese and Japanese are counted by character.

Generated pages have their quotation marks, apostrophes, dashes and spacing set the way the course language sets them before they are stored. Punctuation in the inspector applies the same rules to one page by hand; the chapter editor has the same button for a chapter. See Punctuation.
Publish just this page in the inspector sends the selected page to every destination of the course; the chapter editor's Publish chapter does the same for a chapter and its pages. See Publishing.

There are three ways to have CourseForge write pages, and the difference that matters is not live versus batch - it is browser versus server. Who does the work Close the tab? Price Needs In this tab the browser, N pages at a time no normal nothing In the background CourseForge, from the scheduler yes normal the scheduler As a batch the provider's own queue yes about half a :batch model and the scheduler The first is right for three pages you are watching: it starts immediately and you see each page land. The other two are runs. A run is written down on the server before any work starts, so it survives the tab, the session and a restart. The Content tab shows it as a card with its own progress; reopen the course tomorrow and the card is still there, still counting.

On the Content tab, choose what to write (all missing pages, the next N, the failed ones, everything) and click the run button. It offers whichever kind the profile is set up for: the page model has :batch on the end (the batch queue switch on Profiles › Models & output) - the run goes to the provider's queue; otherwise - a background run, written by the scheduler. Until the scheduler is set up and calling in, the Content tab does not offer runs at all, and says why.

A background run is worked by cron.php, one tick a minute. Each tick claims a page, writes it with the profile's page model, stores it, and moves on until its time is up; a page is stored the moment it is finished, so a tick cut short by a host time limit loses nothing. How many pages are written at once is the scheduler's worker count (app.cron_workers): with two workers, a tick that arrives while the previous one is still busy takes the second slot, and roughly twice as many pages get written. Raise it only as far as your provider's rate limits allow - the failure mode of too many workers is a run full of 429 errors, not a faster course. See The scheduler. A page that fails is retried on a later tick, up to the configured number of attempts, and then marked failed with the provider's reason.

Provider batch APIs answer within a day instead of straight away, and cost about half as much. CourseForge exposes that through a suffix on the page model: text Copyclaude-sonnet-5-5:batch gpt-6-luna:batch anthropic/claude-opus-5:batch The suffix is CourseForge's own marker, not part of any provider's model id. It is stripped before the request goes out, only ever from the end, so an OpenRouter slug such as deepseek/deepseek-r1:free survives untouched. A profile switches between live and queued generation by editing one string, or by ticking the box. Regenerating one page from the editor always runs live, whatever the slot says - waiting a day for a page you are looking at would be absurd. The outline is never batched either; it is one call.

Submitted. CourseForge builds every page's prompt, packs them into the provider's queue format - in as many chunks as the provider's limits require - and submits them. The run records the provider's batch id. Polled. The scheduler asks the provider how far the batch has got, no more often than the polling interval in Settings › Batch and runs. Check the run on the card (or poll_run over MCP) asks immediately. Collected. Finished answers are written into the database as they arrive. A page that came back refused or cut off is marked failed with the reason, exactly as a live page would be. Closed. When the provider reports the batch done, the run closes. Failed pages can be retried with Retry the failed pages. A batch answer that arrives for a page somebody has since written another way is discarded rather than applied, and reported as already written.

Provider Queue Notes Anthropic Message Batches Requests inline in one body. Results can be very large; CourseForge streams them line by line. OpenAI Batch API Upload a JSONL file, poll, download two result files (successes and failures). Google Gemini Batch mode (paid tier) A long-running operation. Expires after 48 hours with no results at all if not finished. OpenRouter Batch beta Requests inline; answers come back in the status response. No cancel route. Groq and probed presets OpenAI-shaped file queue Whether a gateway has a queue is asked of the endpoint with your key, not assumed. Mistral, local servers none Mistral's own queue is not OpenAI-shaped; Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and llama.cpp have none. Check this account on the profile records what the queue can do for your key. Whether an account can queue right now is three questions: does the adapter implement a queue, did the probe find one for this key, and does the provider say its queue takes this model. The profile's batch switch is disabled with the reason when the answer is no.

Provider Unfinished work expires Results downloadable until Anthropic 24 h after creation (unbilled) 29 days OpenAI and file queues 24 h (Groq also offers 7 days) 30 days Gemini 48 h, and then nothing is returned six weeks OpenRouter 24 h 30 days No provider is durable storage. CourseForge writes answers into its own database as they arrive and polls runs nearest their download deadline first - but only while the scheduler is running.

Before a large run, the estimate (and estimate_run over MCP) answers what the run would do: how many pages, which model and provider, background or queue, and roughly how many input and output tokens. The input figure is measured from the real prompts the run would send - sampled across the selection and scaled up - and the answer says how many pages were measured. It gives no price, because CourseForge does not know what your account pays; multiply by your provider's per-token price. The warning worth reading is the one that says the provider has a queue you are not using.

Stop run on the card: A background run stops immediately: the run closes, and every page not yet written is released. A batch is stopped at the provider's pace. The cancel is asynchronous and the provider keeps whatever it finished before the request landed, so the run stays open until the provider reports the batch cancelled. The next check then collects the finished pages, releases the ones that never ran, and closes the run. OpenRouter has no cancel route; a run there stays open and says so. A finished run's card can be removed with Remove run; old run records are cleaned up after the retention period in Settings › Batch and runs.

Streaming. Pages are requested whole and stored when complete; progress is shown per page, not per token. Webhooks. Batches are collected by polling from the scheduler, which also works on hosts nothing inbound can reach. AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure. No account type; put a LiteLLM proxy in front of them.

estimate_run, start_run, list_runs, get_run, poll_run, cancel_run, delete_run and scheduler_status. This is the group that spends money at scale - narrow a connection's scopes if it does not need it. See the MCP tool reference.

Every page is assembled from elements that can be switched on or off - a summary, exercises, diagrams, formulas, Anki cards - and values that size them: minimum and maximum length, how many exercises, for which audience. Both are decided at five levels and inherited downwards. Each level either decides or inherits. Only the levels that decide store anything. Level Where Typical use Installation config/defaults.json, overridden on Administration › Settings › Course defaults The baseline for a whole installation that teaches one subject to one audience. Profile Profiles › Content defaults A house style shared by every course written with that profile. Course The course's Details tab What this course needs. Chapter The Content tab's inspector with a chapter selected A chapter of exercises, a chapter without code. Page The Content tab's inspector, details tab The one page that needs a diagram budget of five. The Details tab. Each element row has a three-way switch; each value shows your number or the inherited one, greyed.

Below the installation, every element has a three-way switch: Position Meaning ↳ on / ↳ off inherit - the arrow shows what the level above currently resolves to On force on, here and for everything below Off force off, here and for everything below A value box shows your own number, or nothing with the inherited number as a greyed placeholder; the ✕ goes back to inheriting. A value whose element is currently off is dimmed, because it changes nothing. Only deviations are stored. A course with nothing overridden carries an empty settings object, so changing a default reaches every course that never disagreed with it - including new defaults that an update brings. The Details tab says where its "inherit" points: the profile "House style" or the installation defaults, with a button to open the profile. The Details tab also lists every chapter and page that overrides something, with a one-click way to make it follow the course again.

Element Default What it adds to a page Learning objectives off Opens the page with a short list of what the reader will be able to do afterwards. Summary section on Closes the page with a compact recap of the key points. Practice exercises on Adds hands-on tasks with worked solutions. Uses the "Exercises per page" value. Key terms glossary off Adds a short glossary of the terms introduced on this page. Further reading off Points to official documentation, standards or classic references. Code examples on Allows fenced, runnable code samples with language identifiers. Comparison tables on Allows Markdown tables for comparisons, options and overviews. Note / Tip / Warning callouts on Allows blockquote callouts for the remarks that really matter. Mermaid diagrams on Allows ```mermaid blocks for flows, states, hierarchies and timelines. MathJax formulas on Allows LaTeX formulas using the delimiters BookStack renders. Emojis on Allows a handful of emojis in headings, callouts and do/don't markers. Anki cloze cards off Appends an importable cloze-deletion card set. Uses the "Anki cards" value. Auto links off Lets the AI drop (🔗 Title) cross references, which CourseForge turns into real BookStack links after publishing. Web research off Look up the current state of the topic before writing - latest versions, current documentation, recent releases - and cite what was found. Costs money on most providers, and a client connected over MCP does its own searching instead. Switching an element off is not the same as leaving it out: CourseForge sends an explicit instruction not to produc

Value Default Placeholder What it sizes Minimum length 3000 words {{min_length}} Lower bound for the body of a page. 0 leaves it to the model. Maximum length 15000 words {{max_length}} Upper bound for the body of a page. 0 leaves it to the model. Diagrams per page 2 max {{diagram_max}} Upper bound for Mermaid diagrams. Only used when diagrams are enabled. Exercises per page 3 tasks {{exercise_count}} How many practice tasks a page gets. Only used when exercises are enabled. Anki cards per page 5 cards {{anki_cards}} How many cloze cards a page gets. Only used when Anki cards are enabled. Empty means the model derives it from the course topic. The length contract asks for a page between the minimum and maximum. A value can be left empty at every level, in which case its instruction is not sent.

Administration › Settings › Course defaults shows every element and value, drawn the way the Details tab draws them but with a two-way switch, because there is nothing above the installation to inherit from. Changing one writes an override into data/config.json and leaves the shipped config/defaults.json alone. Reset drops the override and hands the decision back to the release. WarningBecause only deviations are stored below the installation, changing a course default moves every course, chapter and page that never disagreed with it. That is the point - but it is worth knowing before you change one on an installation with courses already in it.

The catalogue lives in config/defaults.json under details, as features and params. A new element is one entry there plus its two prompt slots - no code change, no migration. Its settings row, its Details row and its MCP support appear by themselves.

Tool Does get_detail_catalogue Every element and value with its default and description. get_details What applies at one level (course, chapter or page) and where each answer comes from. set_details / reset_details Decide or go back to inheriting. Features as 1, -1 or 0. list_detail_overrides Every chapter and page that overrides anything, in one call. set_profile_details The same for a profile. The installation baseline is reached with set_settings, by the keys details.features.<element>.default and details.params.<value>.default.
Models are trained on the past. A course about a library written from a model's memory teaches the version it remembers, which may be two releases old. Web research fixes that, at two levels.

Switch the Web research element on for a page, chapter or course (Content details) and the page is written against what the web says today, with a ## Sources list at the end. The Searches per page value caps how many searches the model may run (0 lets it decide). That needs a provider with a server-side search tool: Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, and the OpenAI models that have one. It is right for "is this example still the recommended way?", and it is paid for on every page.

h: At course level: the research briefing
t: "Which version of WordPress is this course about?" is one fact, and every page needs the same answer. Asking two hundred pages to find it separately gets two hundred answers and pays for the search two hundred times. So a course carries a research briefing: findings established once, stored with the date they were established, and read from then on by the outline and by every page. A briefing is headings, bullets and a list of sources: markdown Copy## Versions - Python 3.14 is the current release; scikit-learn 1.9 and pandas 3 are current. - PyTorch 2.11 is current. ## Deprecated - `pandas.DataFrame.append` is gone; use `pd.concat`. ## Sources - https://scikit-learn.org/stable/whats_new.html

Who How An MCP client - Claude Code most usefully get_research_brief → it searches with its own tools → store_research. The searching happens inside a subscription you already pay for; the server spends nothing. A provider with a search tool Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter and the OpenAI models that have one, when web research is on at course level. You Course › Details › Research: a split editor with the Markdown on the left and the rendered briefing on the right. Nothing downstream can tell the three apart.

With web research on at course level, research comes before the outline - the outline is designed from the findings, because a chapter list built around a version that no longer exists cannot be repaired by researching the pages under it. Over MCP, get_next_step reports the state needs_research until findings are stored. text Copycreate_course(web_research: true) get_next_step → "needs_research" get_research_brief → the assignment: the current stable version and its date, what changed recently enough that a model would get it wrong, what was deprecated and what replaced it, where the documentation lives now (the client searches the web) store_research → stored, stamped with today's date get_structure_brief → the findings are part of the outline prompt get_page_brief → every page carries them

Every answer says how old the findings are - stored today, stored 12 days ago, stored 3 month(s) ago - worth refreshing - because a six-month-old note about a stable subject still beats a model's recollection, and deciding when it is too stale depends on how fast the subject moves. Storing again replaces what is there.

A briefing is cut at 12,000 characters, at a line boundary. The cap exists because the briefing rides in the context of every page: twelve thousand characters is about three thousand tokens, and a five-hundred-page course pays for it five hundred times (much of it from the prompt cache, see Tokens and caching).

The briefing reaches the prompts through the research_block slot in the Course structure group, which renders {{research_block}} (the findings with their date wrapped around them) or {{research_findings}} for a wording of your own. A course with no findings contributes nothing at all, rather than a heading over an empty section. app.research_default_searches (8 by default, under Settings › General) is the search budget quoted for researching a whole course when the course names none of its own.
Tags are a reusable library (Tags in the sidebar) that can be attached to a course, a chapter or a page. What reaches BookStack is each item's effective set: its own tags plus the ones it inherits.

On the outline: a {{Tag, Tag}} marker behind a title, or on the line below it, tags the book, a chapter or a page when the outline is applied. On the Content tab: the inspector's tags tab, for the selected chapter or page. On the course: Settings › Course tags. A tag can carry a value as well as a name, which BookStack shows as name: value.

A tag marked as inheriting flows down: from the course to every chapter and page, from a chapter to its pages. Use it for what is true of everything below - the subject, the audience, the version a course covers. Leave it off for tags that describe one page.

Switch on AI tagging on the course's Settings tab and the model proposes tags while it designs the outline. They appear in violet, and each can be deactivated individually without being deleted. A deactivated tag is ignored everywhere: in prompts, in the fingerprints that decide whether a page is in sync, and in BookStack. AI tagging never re-enables a tag you deactivated and never downgrades one you attached by hand. You can restrict the AI to a tag pool - the tags it may choose from - optionally strictly, so it may not invent new ones.

A tag's name and value are part of what CourseForge fingerprints to decide whether a page is out of sync with BookStack. Changing a tag, or its value, marks the pages that carry it as changed, and the next push rewrites them.

list_tags, create_tag, update_tag, delete_tag, get_course_tags, attach_tag, detach_tag and set_tag_link. For an administrator, list_tags returns every account's tags, each marked with its owner. See the MCP tool reference.

A model writing German opens a quotation with „ and closes it with ". The mistake is too small to notice on one page and it is on every page of a five-hundred-page book. CourseForge fixes it with code rather than with a sentence in a prompt, because a rule that runs beats a rule that is asked for.

A generated page has its punctuation set before it is stored: Language Written Stored German „Wort", **"Wort"**, Wort—Wort „Wort“, **„Wort“**, Wort – Wort French "mot", « mot », mot ; « mot » with narrow spaces, mot ; Spanish, Italian, Greek "parola" «parola» Polish, Hungarian "słowo" „słowo” Czech, Slovak "slovo" „slovo“ Russian, Ukrainian "слово" «слово» Swedish, Finnish "ord" ”ord” English and the rest "word", don't, '90s “word”, don’t, ’90s every language ..., a - b, 1990-2000, 5" …, a – b, 1990–2000, 5″ every language zwei Wörter , and three blank lines one space, , against the word, one blank line A language CourseForge does not recognise is set the English way. The course language is free text, so it is recognised rather than validated; a two-letter code only matches exactly (es is Spanish, Estonian is not).

Anything that is not prose: fenced code blocks, inline code, links and their targets, bare addresses, HTML tags and comments, formulas, a table's alignment row, characters escaped on purpose, cross-reference markers and cloze deletions. They are lifted out before the rules run and put back exactly as they were. A curly quote inside a JSON example is not typography, it is a broken example. It reads a quotation mark the way a reader does: by position first (a mark glued to text on one side has said which side it is on, stepping over Markdown emphasis), by depth second, and by the glyph last. Nested quotations come out as „… ‚…‘ …“ whatever was typed. It is idempotent - a page set twice is byte-for-byte the page set once - and bounded: quotation depth is forgotten at every block boundary, so one unbalanced mark can confuse its own paragraph and nothing after it. It runs where a page is stored, which is where all three roads meet: the in-tab generator, a background or batch run, and a page an MCP client stored with write_page. It never touches the outline's titles, because titles are matched byte for byte when an outline is applied.
Each profile decides: Profiles › Models & output › Correct the punctuation of a generated page. A profile that has never decided follows app.typography on Administration › Settings, which is on.

h: Correcting a course that is already written
t: Pages stored before this existed, with the setting off, or under older and worse rules, can be corrected on a button, at three scopes: the whole course: Course › Settings › Punctuation; a chapter and its pages: Punctuation beside Publish chapter in the chapter editor; one page: Punctuation in the inspector. It asks first. The button runs the whole pass with writing switched off and reports the exact number that would change - "of 41 pages and 6 chapters, this would change 12 pages and 1 chapter", naming the first forty - and only then offers to do it. It runs whatever the profile's switch says: pressing the button is an instruction, not a preference. It touches every page's Markdown and title, every chapter's title and goal, and the book's title and description, then rewrites the outline from the corrected titles. A page's extra context and the research briefing are left alone - they are instructions to the writer, not text anybody reads. It costs nothing: no model is called. A corrected page differs from the published one, so it shows as out of sync until the next push. A page that needed nothing is not written at all and does not go out of sync.

fix_typography with course_id, an optional chapter_id or page_id (a page wins over a chapter, which wins over the course), an optional language, and preview to see what would change without changing it.

The Publish tab sends a course into BookStack over its REST API: the book on a shelf, every chapter, every written page with its effective tags, and real links for every cross reference. Publishing again sends only what changed. The All destinations card, one card per destination, and the publish log.

A destination is one BookStack instance from the course's profile, with its own shelf and its own book. A course may have several - a staging wiki and the live one, or the wikis of two departments. Add destination and pick one of the profile's BookStack instances. Load shelves to fetch that wiki's shelves, and pick the one the book belongs on. Save. Each destination has a switch: off keeps everything already published there on record and simply leaves it out of the next push. Remove is something else, and the dialog says so: CourseForge forgets the book it made there, so publishing to that instance again later creates a second book beside the first. Pointing a destination at a different instance costs the same and asks the same question - to publish to both, add a second destination instead. NoteThe course Settings tab and the MCP update_course tool still take a single BookStack instance, because for most courses "where does this publish" has one answer. They set the first destination; anything behind it is left alone.

The All destinations card speaks for every destination that is switched on: Publish everything - the book, its shelf, every chapter and every page that has text. Publish the book - only the book and its shelf, which is what a renamed course needs. Force overwrite - re-sends even items that have not changed. That is also what repairs a page somebody edited by hand in BookStack. Resolve auto links - rewrites cross-reference markers into links without a full push. See Auto links. Each destination's own card has Publish here, Book only and Resolve links here, acting on that wiki alone - the answer to one wiki having been down while the others were fine. Single pages and chapters can be published from the Content tab: Publish just this page in the inspector, Publish chapter in the chapter editor.

Creates the book once, puts it on the shelf, and updates it in place from then on. Creates or updates every chapter and page, in order, with its effective tags (own plus inherited). Pages without content are skipped. Skips everything whose fingerprint matches what was last pushed to that wiki. Recreates an item that was deleted in BookStack. Any error other than a genuine 404 aborts that wiki's push rather than risking a duplicate. At the end of a full push, resolves cross references into links in every page that has them. Nothing is ever duplicated: every item is created once and updated afterwards, and what is fingerprinted is exactly what is sent - resolved links included - so the sync badges never drift from reality.

Pressing a publish button writes a task down and returns at once. The scheduler works it in slices of one tick each, so you can close the tab, or the laptop. A push interrupted half way - a wiki that stopped answering, a host time limit, a process that died - is picked up again from the page it stopped at, never from the start: every item is written and recorded before the next one is looked at. Attempts are spaced out: half a minute, a minute, two, five, ten, up to a quarter of an hour, and given up after app.task_max_attempts (twenty by default). One wiki failing does not stop the others, and only the failed one is tried again. Retry on a task that was given up or stopped carries on from where it got to. Stop ends one, keeping whatever was already written. A course never has two tasks worked at once, because a publish and a link pass on the same wiki would write the same pages over each other. On an installation whose scheduler is not set up - or has stopped calling in - the open tab works a queued task itself, one bounded slice per request, and says so in a yellow strip. Setting up the scheduler is what lets a push carry on with the tab closed.

The log is the server's. Every line a task says - created, updated, skipped, recreated, the link pass, a failure in the wiki's own words - is written down as it is said and shown whenever the tab is opened, grouped under its task with who asked, when, which attempt this is and the state of each wiki. It is the record of what happened while nobody was watching. Clear forgets finished tasks; the thirty most recent are kept per course regardless.

Per wiki: the book and shelf, pages published, out of sync, never published, cross references, and the last outcome. Each destination's card shows its book and shelf, how many pages it holds, how many are out of sync, how many written pages it does not hold at all, how its cross references resolve - each wiki resolves them against its own book - and what last happened to it: published a minute ago, failed and trying again, failed and given up, with the reason. The All destinations card folds the counts across every destination that is switched on: published everywhere means published in every one of them, and out of sync somewhere means at least one would be written to. Adding a second destination to a finished course therefore lights up immediately, which is exactly the state it is in.

For code highlighting, Mermaid diagrams, formulas and embeds in BookStack itself, give the wiki a BookStackDev look.

set_publish_targets, publish_course (with part: "book" for the book alone), resolve_links, get_publish_status and list_unresolved_links. Over MCP, publish_course runs the push to the end inside the call rather than as a task. See the MCP tool reference.

Switch the Auto links element on for a course (Content details) and the AI marks cross references to other chapters and pages while it writes: markdown CopyThe reactive system (🔗 Reactive state with ref and reactive) does this for you. At that moment it is plain text, and it needs to be: when page 3 is written, page 40 may not exist in BookStack yet. The Auto links per page value caps how many a page may contain.

After a course has been published, CourseForge walks every page and rewrites the markers into real links - programmatically, with no second AI call: markdown CopyThe reactive system ([🔗 Reactive state with ref and reactive](https://wiki.example.com/books/vue/page/reactive-state-with-ref-and-reactive)) does this for you. It runs automatically at the end of every full publish, and on demand from Publish › Resolve auto links (or Resolve links here on one destination). Only pages whose text actually changed are re-sent. Each destination resolves links against its own book, because the same page has a different address in every wiki.
the title exactly as written; a normalised comparison - case, punctuation and spacing ignored; a unique prefix - (🔗 Reactivity) finds Reactivity in depth; the closest match above a similarity floor.
