h: Why it is safe to run as often as you like
t: The stored page keeps the raw marker. Resolution happens on the way out, so it is repeatable, survives a regeneration and can never corrupt the source text. Renaming a target turns its stale references back into plain text rather than pointing them at the wrong page. What is fingerprinted is what is sent. The out-of-sync badges account for resolved links, so a link change is detected exactly once and never loops. The Content tab shows a link icon on every page that carries markers; the course header and the Publish tab show resolved / written for the whole course. Over MCP, list_unresolved_links lists the markers that did not resolve.

BookStack renders a page well, and a course better with a little help: code that is highlighted, a fenced mermaid block that becomes a diagram, \( … \) that becomes a formula, a YouTube link on its own line that becomes the video. BookStackDev is that help - a loader script plus the CSS and JavaScript modules it fetches, pasted into BookStack as one line under Settings › Customization › Custom HTML head content. CourseForge's prompts write for a wiki wearing it, which is why it is managed in CourseForge rather than beside it. A look: every feature is a card with a switch; the defaults are BookStackDev's own.

A look is one BookStackDev configuration, kept in CourseForge and served to every wiki allowed to load it. Open BookStackDev in the sidebar and click New look. A look has three tabs: Features, Link & wikis and Conventions.

Every value of BookStackDev's configuration has a field, grouped into nine cards, each with its switch. The defaults are the ones the standalone BookStackDev ships with, so a new look renders a wiki exactly as BookStackDev itself would. Feature What it does Worth knowing Code blocks Shiki highlighting in about 220 languages, each grammar fetched the first time it is needed, with line numbers, wrapping, a copy button and a collapse for tall blocks Light and dark themes are any Shiki themes. A block with no language is recognised by CourseForge's own detector first, highlight.js second. Mermaid diagrams A fenced mermaid block drawn as a diagram, following the wiki's light or dark mode A theme per mode MathJax formulas TeX typeset in the page Which delimiters count: \( … \) and $$ … $$ by default, $ … $ off so a price stays a price Light and dark toggle A floating button Corner, distance, size Page styling Zoom, softer text, an optional background image Link embeds A link alone in its paragraph becomes the video, track or pen it points at Only on a page view, by default Audio player An .mp3 or .m4a link becomes an inline player External links Marked with an arrow and opened in a new tab Hosts to treat as internal Markdown editor A single newline becomes a line break in BookStack's editor preview Each card's advanced fields - module URLs, selectors, the debug switch - are folded away for the wiki that is unusual.

This tab shows the one line to paste into BookStack: html Copy<script src="https://your-install/bs.php?k=<key>" crossorigin="anonymous"></script> bs.php serves the loader with the look's settings written in front of it, and every module and stylesheet the loader fetches comes back through the same endpoint. Each of those requests carries the origin of the wiki page that made it - that is what crossorigin="anonymous" is for - and the endpoint answers only an origin the look allows. Any other gets a 403 naming the wiki, and the browser refuses to run what it did not get permission for. So the key is not a secret - it sits in the head of every wiki page. What keeps the line honest is the list of allowed wikis: Your BookStack instances: on Profiles › Accounts, each instance card has a Look select. An instance wearing a look is allowed by its base URL. Other wikis: origins typed in by hand, such as https://docs.partner.example, for a wiki CourseForge holds no credentials for. One look serves any number of wikis, and there is nothing to copy per wiki but the line. Regenerate the link issues a new key and retires the old one, for the day a line was pasted somewhere it should not have been; the allowed wikis keep their permission and get the new line.

Every prompt that mentions a formula, a diagram or a code fence is written for BookStackDev's defaults: formulas as \( … \) and $$ … $$, diagrams as fenced mermaid, code in fenced blocks. Change those in a look and the wiki renders one thing while the prompts ask for another. Conventions compares the look with the prompts of every profile whose instance wears it - the profile's override where there is one, the installation's prompt otherwise - and lists each disagreement with the wording that would resolve it. The same note appears on the profile's Prompts tab and the administration Prompts screen, on the slot concerned, with a button that applies the recommended text where it belongs.

bs.php is the third public PHP file, beside api/index.php and cron.php; the nginx and Caddy configurations on Security already hand every .php file to PHP, and .htaccess needs nothing. Assets are served with a long cache life and an ETag, and the version in every asset URL changes with each CourseForge release, so a wiki picks up an update on its next page load. The files served are those in assets/bookstackdev/ - the standalone BookStackDev folder, unchanged. The loader reads its configuration from the object CourseForge writes in front of it, or from its own CONFIG block when used standalone. Shiki, highlight.js, Mermaid, MathJax and the optional Font Awesome glyphs are fetched by the reader's browser from public CDNs, on the versions current at this release: Shiki 4, highlight.js 11, Mermaid 12, MathJax 4 and Font Awesome 7. Mermaid is pinned to the 11.x layout and look, so diagrams do not suddenly change size. For a wiki that must not reach a CDN, the module URLs are advanced fields on the cards; point them at copies you host.

Under the profiles scope: list_bookstackdev_profiles, list_bookstackdev_options, get_bookstackdev_profile, create_bookstackdev_profile, update_bookstackdev_profile, delete_bookstackdev_profile, rotate_bookstackdev_link and check_bookstackdev_conventions, plus bookstackdev_id on update_profile and add_bookstack_instance.

CourseForge reaches a model through an AI account on a profile. There are five types: four native adapters and one for everything else that speaks OpenAI's /chat/completions. Type Endpoint Batch queue Credential Anthropic API POST /v1/messages yes, Message Batches sk-ant- key OpenAI POST /v1/chat/completions yes, file upload API key Google Gemini (beta) POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent yes, paid tier only Gemini API key OpenRouter POST /api/v1/chat/completions yes, /api/beta/batches OpenRouter key A preset or a custom endpoint POST {base}/chat/completions if the endpoint has one - asked, not assumed API key, or none for a local server All of them work on an ordinary web host.

Because all four providers report at least one kind of failure with an HTTP 200, and in every case the body would otherwise be stored as a course page. A blank page, or one that stops mid-sentence, looks like work that succeeded. Each adapter knows its provider's version of: A refusal or a safety block - Anthropic answers one at 200; Gemini returns no candidates and a blockReason. An answer cut off by the output limit - stop_reason, finishReason: MAX_TOKENS (or RECITATION, frequent for long educational prose), finish_reason: length. Every one arrives with most of a lesson attached. An upstream error reported at 200 by a gateway that fans out. A routed provider that failed after it started - OpenRouter commits the 200 as soon as the model starts producing. Every one of those raises an error with the provider's reason instead of storing half a page, on the live path and the batch path alike.

Speaks API version 2026-10-21, which refuses temperature, top_p and top_k on every model, so none is sent: the profile's temperature does not apply to Claude. What differs between models is read from the models endpoint's capabilities object - whether the batch queue takes a model and how long an answer it can produce - never from the model's name. The list is cached for a day. When the endpoint cannot be reached, the picker falls back to claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5. The shared part of every page prompt carries cache breakpoints, so pages after the first read it from the prompt cache. A one-off request (an outline, a scope plan) gets none, because a cache write costs a quarter more and would never be read. Batches use the one-hour cache. See Tokens and caching. Results of large batches are streamed line by line, so a gigabyte of prose never has to fit in PHP's memory.

Reasoning models - the GPT-5 and GPT-6 families (gpt-6-sol, gpt-6-luna, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6.1-terra…) and the o-series - take max_completion_tokens and refuse temperature, top_p, the penalties, logit_bias and logprobs. CourseForge decides that from the model id, because OpenAI's model list carries no capability data; a model released after that rule was written costs one retry, because a 400 that blames a parameter is retried once without it. The model picker is curated - /v1/models mixes embeddings, audio, images and every fine-tune in with the chat models - but only when the address really is api.openai.com. Prompt caching: prompt_cache_key keeps a course's pages where its cache is warm. On gpt-5.6 and later, which bill cache writes, CourseForge sets explicit cache points behind each shared part so only the shared part is written.

WarningGemini is offered as beta because Google is migrating API keys. Unrestricted standard keys are already rejected, standard keys were expected to stop working altogether in September 2026, and their replacement - the service-account-bound key with an AQ. prefix - has an open cluster of reports of answering 401 ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED. So the adapter never collapses a Gemini error into "authentication failed": it shows Google's own error envelope verbatim, which is the only way to tell a wrong key from a key type the endpoint will not take. Not OpenAI-shaped in any particular: the model is in the URL path, authentication is an x-goog-api-key header, the system prompt is a top-level systemInstruction, and answers come back in candidates[]. The batch queue is paid-tier only and accepts a published list of models, including gemini-4-argon and gemini-3.8-flash. A batch still running after 48 hours expires with no results at all. Caching is implicit: the shared part of every prompt opens the system instruction, which is what Gemini's cache keys on (4,096 tokens minimum on current models).

One key for every vendor OpenRouter fronts. Model ids carry a vendor prefix (anthropic/claude-opus-5); routing suffixes such as :free or :nitro are typed in by hand rather than offered in the picker. Sixty-odd real OpenRouter slugs end in :batch, which collides with CourseForge's marker. The adapter splits a slug on its last colon and always sends the plain one upstream, so both readings agree. Batches go to the beta endpoint, which has no cancel route: a stopped run there stays open until the provider is done. Caching: cache_control markers for Claude, Gemini and Qwen upstreams, and prompt_cache_key for every model, which OpenRouter also uses to keep a course on one upstream provider.

Many gateways claim OpenAI compatibility, and the claim is true about the chat body. Everything around it differs - Groq hangs its API under /openai/v1 and rejects logprobs, DeepInfra lives at /v1/openai, Z.ai has no /v1 at all, Ollama takes any key or none. That is configuration, so it is one class and a table: picking a preset fills in the base URL, the parameters that gateway refuses, what its output limit is called and whether it might have a queue. h: Asking an endpoint whether it has a queue
t: Rather than keep a list of which gateways have a batch API, CourseForge asks: three GETs, and where the answer is still ambiguous one POST of an empty object that every real queue rejects with a validation error. Nothing is created and no chat request is made - which matters for local servers, where naming a model that is not loaded can block for minutes while gigabytes load. The answer belongs to the account, not the preset, because the same address behaves differently per key. It is stored on the account and taken again when the key or address changes, when it is a month old, or when a real submission proves it wrong. Two verdicts earn the feature its keep: a queue with no upload lane (Gemini's compatibility layer answers /batches and 404s /files), and forbidden, as distinct from absent (Gemini's queue is paid-tier only, and a 403 must not disable batching for an account that only needs an upgrade).

Outline slot: your strongest model. It is one request per course, and every page inherits its quality through the scopes. Page slot: a capable mid-range model is usually the best trade. Try three pages in the tab before starting a run of three hundred. Batch: if you can wait a day, the batch switch halves the price of the page slot on every provider that has a queue. Local: a local model is free per token and fine for drafting outlines; make sure its context window holds the course map.

AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Azure have no account type: each uses an authentication scheme of its own rather than a bearer key. Put a LiteLLM proxy in front of them and use the litellm preset. Streaming and webhooks - see Runs. Mistral's own batch queue, which is not OpenAI-shaped. Mistral is live-only. A Claude Pro/Max subscription as an AI account. Releases 4.0-5.0 offered one, which ran the claude CLI on the same machine; it only ever worked on a laptop and was retired in 5.1. To use a subscription with a hosted CourseForge, turn it around: connect the Claude app or Claude Code over MCP and let it do the writing.

A page is written in a request of its own, so it knows about the rest of the course exactly what its prompt tells it. Two goals pull against each other here: a page should know enough about the others not to repeat them, and every page pays for whatever it is told. Since 5.3 CourseForge gets both.

What every page owns. The outline carries a scope under every page, and the page prompt carries the course map: every chapter, and every page numbered chapter.page with its title and scope. text Copy1. Foundations 1.1 What a model learns - Supervised and unsupervised learning; features and labels 1.2 Setting up the toolkit - Python 3.14 with uv; NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn 2. Your first models 2.1 Linear regression - The hypothesis; least squares; reading coefficients 2.2 Gradient descent - The loss surface; the update rule; learning rate The model writing 2.1 can see that the update rule belongs to 2.2 and leave it there, naming that page instead of teaching it. The scopes are planned once, together, when the outline is designed - the one moment anything sees the whole course at once. Its own chapter. The chapter's goal goes with every page of that chapter, and only that chapter's. What its neighbours actually say. When pages of the same chapter are already written, the brief lists them with their section headings, read from the stored text. Plans drift; headings show where. They cost one line per heading, no extra request, and only the same chapter is shown - which is where overlap happens. A batch submits every page at once, so it has no written neighbours and relies on the map alone.

Providers cache the beginning of a prompt: if a request starts with exactly the same bytes as a recent one, that prefix is read back at a fraction of the price. So CourseForge puts everything shared first, byte-identical for every page that shares it, and everything that differs last. The shared part comes first and is identical from page to page; only the short brief at the end is paid in full. Provider What CourseForge sends Anthropic A cache breakpoint behind the course map, the chapter and the system text. A request sent once - an outline, a scope plan - gets none, because a cache write costs a quarter more and would never be read. Batches use the one-hour cache. OpenAI (gpt-5.6 and later) An explicit cache point behind each shared part and prompt_cache_options.mode: explicit, so only the shared part is written - these models bill cache writes. Plus prompt_cache_key, which keeps a course's pages where its cache is warm. Earlier models: the key, and the shared part first. Google Gemini The shared parts open the system instruction, which is what implicit caching keys on (4,096 tokens minimum on current models). OpenRouter cache_control markers for Claude, Gemini and Qwen upstreams, and prompt_cache_key for every model. Everything else The shared part first, in one system message - the order any automatic prefix cache needs. ImportantIf you edit the prompt library, keep anything that differs from page to page in page_user, never in the shared segments or in page_system. One changed byte early in a prompt is a cache miss for everything after it. See The prompt library.

Measured on a course of 20 chapters × 7 pages with six-hundred-word chapter descriptions, all pages written, building every page's prompt with the old code and the new: Per page 5.2 5.3 Prompt size 138,832 characters (about 35,000 tokens) 47,464 characters (about 12,000 tokens) Identical for every page of the course or chapter the system text, and only when no page had tags 35,727 characters Building the prompt 18 ms, 10 MB peak 7 ms, 6 MB peak That is two thirds less input before any cache, and with Anthropic's cache reading the shared part at a tenth of the price, a little over nine tenths less billed input on a live run. Building a prompt also stopped reading the text of every page of the course, which a batch used to do once per page. 5.2's single cache breakpoint sat on a part of the prompt that differed for every page as soon as pages had tags, so it paid the cache-write premium on every page and was never read back. That is the kind of mistake the byte-identical-prefix rule exists to prevent.

h: Over MCP: sending the map once
t: A client writing a whole course in one conversation would otherwise receive the course map with every page brief. get_page_brief hands the shared parts out separately, each with an id; a client that passes the ids back as known_context is not sent the same text again. For a hundred-page course that is the difference between the map entering the client's context once and entering it a hundred times. See Connect an AI client.

Plan scopes. A course with scopes writes better pages and the scopes are what make the map useful. Plan missing scopes on the Structure tab fills them in for an older outline in one request. Write in chapter order when writing live, so later pages see their neighbours' headings. Use the batch queue for whole courses you can wait a day for: about half price on top of caching where the provider caches batch requests. Keep the research briefing short. It rides in the shared part of every page (cached, but not free). Estimate first. estimate_run measures the real prompts and reports tokens before anything is spent. See Runs.

Every instruction CourseForge sends to a model is a named slot. There are 48 of them, they ship in config/defaults.json, and every one can be overridden. Nothing the AI is told is hidden in code, apart from two rules the application depends on: never emit a level-1 heading, never emit raw HTML. Administration › Prompts: group, slot and editor, with the placeholders the slot understands as clickable chips.

Layer Where Who Applies to Installation Administration › Prompts an administrator every course, unless a profile disagrees Profile Profiles › Prompts anybody, on their own profiles the courses that use that profile The profile layer wins. Both screens say so at the top, show the same slots in the same order under the same labels, and mark the ones that have been changed - they are literally the same component. The two layers treat an empty slot differently, on purpose: a profile override that is deliberately empty is honoured: that slot sends nothing, which is how you switch a block of instructions off for one profile's courses; clearing a slot on the installation screen removes the override, so the shipped default applies again. A handful of slots the pipeline cannot work without (page_system, page_rules, page_user, overview_user…) fall back to a compact built-in text rather than sending nothing, whichever layer emptied them.

Both screens are three panes: group, slot, editor. The search ignores the groups, because the usual question is "where is the one about diagrams?". Each slot shows its description and the placeholders it understands as chips; clicking one inserts it at the cursor. The editor is the same CodeMirror the pages use, with {{placeholder}} highlighting. Placeholders are written {{name}}. Substitution only replaces names it knows, so Anki's own cloze syntax {{c1::…}} passes through untouched. If a profile's BookStack instance wears a BookStackDev look whose conventions disagree with a slot - formulas switched off, different delimiters - the slot shows a note with a button that applies the recommended wording.

Group Sent when Global with every request: persona, language reminder, audience Course structure designing or revising an outline, the research briefing, planning page scopes Page writing writing one page: persona, formatting, length, course and chapter context, the brief, written neighbours, feedback Content details one enabled and one disabled text per content detail element

h: How a page prompt is assembled
t: In the order it is sent: text Copyshared = page_context_block the brief, the description, the course map with every page's scope + research_block (only when research is stored) <- the same for every page of the course + page_chapter_block the chapter and its goal <- the same for every page of the chapter system = global_system + audience_block (only when an audience is set) + page_system + page_rules + length_rules (only when a minimum or maximum length is set) + feature_<element>_on|off for every element, in catalogue order + the two hard rules enforced in code + language_instruction user = page_user this page: its place, its scope, its tags, its neighbours + page_written_block (only when pages of its chapter are written: their headings) + extra_context_block (only when the page has extra context) + page_regenerate_user (only on a rewrite with feedback) The shared segments go first and reach the provider separately from the system text, so its prompt cache can stop right behind them (Tokens and caching). Anything that differs from page to page belongs in page_user: one changed byte early in a prompt is a cache miss for everything after it. {{course_structure}} is the compact course map; {{course_structure_full}} is still offered for a library that wants the whole outline, with every chapter description, sent with every page - at the cost the map was built to avoid.

CourseForge has a second front door: an MCP server at api/mcp.php. An AI client that speaks the Model Context Protocol connects to it and can do everything the browser can - create courses, design outlines, write pages, start runs, publish, and for an administrator manage accounts, settings and updates - through 107 tools. It also turns the usual arrangement around. Instead of CourseForge calling a model with an API key, the client does the writing: it asks CourseForge for a page's brief, writes the page itself and stores it. That is how you use a Claude Pro or Max subscription - or any other client's own plan - with a hosted CourseForge, and it costs the server nothing.

Open Connect in the sidebar, give the connection a name ("Laptop - Claude Code"), choose an expiry if you want one (up to a year), and optionally narrow it to some tool groups. Create it, and the screen shows the token once, with a ready-made setup line for each client. Connect: the endpoint, a new connection, and the connections you already have. The token starts with cf4_ and is stored only as a SHA-256 digest; lose it and you make another. Each connection is separate - revoking the laptop does not touch the desktop - and the screen shows when each was last used and how often.
Replace the address and token with the ones the Connect screen gives you. The address is whatever the installation reports (mcp.public_url if set), usually https://your-install/api/mcp.php.

bash Copyclaude mcp add --transport http courseforge https://your-install/api/mcp.php \ --header "Authorization: Bearer cf4_…" Run it in any directory; add --scope user to make the connection available in every project.

In claude_desktop_config.json (Settings › Developer › Edit Config): json Copy{ "mcpServers": { "courseforge": { "type": "http", "url": "https://your-install/api/mcp.php", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer cf4_…" } } } } The desktop app's Settings › Connectors › Add custom connector takes a URL and nothing else, so the Connect screen also offers the token in the address: text Copyhttps://your-install/api/mcp.php?token=cf4_… That form puts a secret into browser history and server logs; prefer the header wherever the client allows it. Custom connectors are reached from the public internet, so a CourseForge on localhost needs a real hostname or a tunnel for them.

In ~/.codex/config.toml, or .codex/config.toml beside a project: toml Copy[mcp_servers.courseforge] url = "https://your-install/api/mcp.php" bearer_token_env_var = "COURSEFORGE_TOKEN" # A page can take minutes to write, and the default is sixty seconds. tool_timeout_sec = 1800 Then export COURSEFORGE_TOKEN=cf4_… in your shell profile. The file holds no secret and is safe to commit.

In .cursor/mcp.json in a project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for all of them: json Copy{ "mcpServers": { "courseforge": { "url": "https://your-install/api/mcp.php", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer cf4_…" } } } } Cursor expands ${env:NAME}, so you can write "Bearer ${env:COURSEFORGE_TOKEN}" and keep the token out of the file.

In .vscode/mcp.json. Note that VS Code calls the top-level object servers, not mcpServers: json Copy{ "servers": { "courseforge": { "type": "http", "url": "https://your-install/api/mcp.php", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer cf4_…" } } } }

In ~/.gemini/settings.json, or .gemini/settings.json beside a project. Gemini CLI calls the address httpUrl; a url would be read as an SSE endpoint, which this is not: json Copy{ "mcpServers": { "courseforge": { "httpUrl": "https://your-install/api/mcp.php", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer cf4_…" } } } }

Any client that speaks streamable HTTP and can send one header can drive CourseForge. To check a token from a terminal: bash Copycurl -sS 'https://your-install/api/mcp.php' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer cf4_…' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'

If you remember one tool, remember get_next_step. It reads the database and says which single call moves a course forward, why, and with what arguments. Because it works the answer out every time, it is right after a restart, a lost context window or a change of client - there is nothing to remember and nothing to resume. whoami is the other first call: who the connection belongs to, its role, and whether the scheduler is running. In practice you rarely call either yourself. You say "write the next three pages of my machine learning course in CourseForge", and the client loops brief → write → store on its own.

Three prompts start a whole job without anybody having to explain the order. In Claude Code they appear as slash commands: Prompt What it does Arguments /mcp__courseforge__build_a_course Take a subject and write a complete course from it - outline, every page, and optionally publish it. CourseForge hands over the briefs and stores the results; the writing happens here, so no AI account has to be configured in CourseForge and nothing is spent on one. topic, name (optional) /mcp__courseforge__continue_a_course Pick up a course that is already started and take it as far as it will go. Works whether it was left after the outline, half written, or finished but unpublished. course_id (optional) /mcp__courseforge__review_a_course Read a finished course and say what is wrong with it - gaps, repetition, pages that contradict each other, chapters in an order that does not teach. Changes nothing. course_id (optional) Each tells the client to call get_next_step and do what it says, rather than reciting steps - which is right in every state, including a course somebody abandoned three weeks ago.

h: Two ways to write a course
t: This is the one decision a model cannot work out from a tool description, which is why the server states it in its own instructions. You write it. get_page_brief hands the client the same prompt CourseForge would send a model: the persona, the formatting rules, the content details resolved for that page, the course map with what every page owns, the page's place and scope, and its neighbours. The client writes the page and stores it with write_page. This spends nothing on the server: the work happens in the client, on your own plan, and CourseForge never holds a credential. A page written this way follows exactly the same rules as one written by the API, so a course can be half written each way and stay coherent. The brief's shared parts - the course map and the chapter - come with ids. Pass them back as known_context on the next call and they are not sent again, so the map enters the client's context once instead of once per page. CourseForge writes it. start_run queues every unwritten page against the course's own AI account and keeps going after the client disconnects - in the background, or through the provider's batch queue at about half price. This spends real money on somebody's provider account, at scale: five hundred pages is five hundred requests. Call estimate_run first. generate_page and generate_structure sit between the two: one call each, billed to the profile, blocking while the model works.

h: Building a course with no AI provider at all
t: CourseForge needs an AI account only if you want CourseForge to do the writing (generate_structure, generate_page, start_run), and a profile only for publishing (which needs BookStack credentials). Everything else - the outline, every page, the content details, the tags - can be done by the client with four tools that need no model, no credential and no profile: text Copyget_structure_brief → the client designs the outline → apply_structure get_page_brief → the client writes the page → write_page On an installation that will never have an AI account, leave Profiles empty.

One thing on this surface is irreversible: applying an outline that would delete pages that already have text. apply_structure works out what would be lost first and refuses unless the client confirms with confirm_removals. A client on protocol revision 2026-07-28 that can ask its user a question gets the question instead: the call pauses (resultType: "input_required"), the client asks you, and repeats the call with the answer. The continuation is signed with HMAC-SHA256, bound to the connection, the account, the tool and a digest of the arguments, expires after fifteen minutes and can be redeemed once - a confirmation for deleting three pages cannot be reused for fifty. Older clients get the refusal naming confirm_removals, as they always did.

CourseForge answers both eras of MCP on one URL: the stateless 2026-07-28 revision (server/discover, resultType, cacheable lists with ttlMs) and the four legacy revisions (initialize, session-style). Which era a request belongs to is read from the request itself and never remembered. The transport is plain HTTP POST; GET and DELETE answer 405. Two client limits it works around: Claude Code truncates a server's instructions at 2 KB, so CourseForge's instructions put the useful part first and stay short. Claude Code truncates a tool result at 25,000 tokens by default, so tools that can return a lot - get_course with include_content is a whole book - declare a larger ceiling in the _meta slot the protocol reserves for it.

The endpoint has no session and no cookie: a bearer token, checked on every request, and 401 for an unknown one. An installation with no connections has no way in at all. A request carrying a browser Origin that is neither this host nor listed in Settings › MCP › allowed origins is refused with 403 - a defence against DNS rebinding. Claude Code, the desktop app and other command-line clients send no Origin and are unaffected. Add an origin only when you really have a browser-based client. Settings › MCP can switch the endpoint off entirely. Signing in, redeeming an invite and first-run setup have no MCP equivalent: they create the credential a tool call needs. revoke_my_connection is the nearest thing to signing out, and it is permanent.

Symptom Likely cause Every request is 401 on Apache Apache drops the Authorization header under CGI/FastCGI. The shipped .htaccess re-exposes it; check it is in place. Or use ?token=. 403 "origin not allowed" A browser-based client: add its exact origin to mcp.allowed_origins. Tool calls time out while a page is written Raise the client's tool timeout (Codex: tool_timeout_sec) and your server's own limit. The client sees fewer tools than expected The connection is narrowed, or the account is not an administrator. list_scopes shows the ceiling. The Claude desktop app cannot reach a local install Custom connectors connect from the internet. Use a public hostname or a tunnel - or the config-file setup above, which runs on your machine. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. confirm_name * string The exact name of the course, as a confirmation that the right one is being deleted.
Take the research assignment for a course, and store what searching the web found. The client does the searching, so nothing here spends anything.

Get the assignment for researching a course readsThe research assignment for a whole course: what to establish about the subject before any of it is designed or written - the current stable version and its release date, what changed recently enough that a model would get it wrong, what has been deprecated and what replaced it, where the official documentation now lives, and what practitioners currently recommend. Search the web from this brief with your own tools, then send what you found to store_research. It is stored once on the course and then read by the outline and by every single page, so a course about something that moves - WordPress, a framework, an API, a standard - is researched one time rather than once per page. Costs nothing: no model is called and no search is run on this server. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.

Store what the research found writesStores the findings from get_research_brief on the course and stamps them with today's date. From then on they travel into the outline brief and into every page brief, and the model is told when they were established so it can say which version a statement holds for. Send Markdown: short sections, dense bullets, and a closing "## Sources" list of what you actually read. Sending an empty string clears the findings. Replaces whatever was stored before - to add to a briefing rather than replace it, read the old one with get_research first and send both. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. findings * string The research findings as Markdown. Anything past 12,000 characters is cut at a line boundary, because this text is carried in the context of every page of the course and is therefore paid for once per page. Send an empty string to clear.

Read the stored research readsThe research findings stored on a course, with the date they were established and how old that makes them. Nothing here ever expires by itself - old findings still beat a guess - so this is what a client reads to decide whether the subject has moved far enough to be worth researching again. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.
Read the outline brief, write an outline, and have CourseForge design one itself.

Get the brief for designing an outline readsThe complete brief for designing a course outline, or for revising the one that already exists: the system instructions and user message CourseForge would send its own model, the course topic, the current outline, the requested changes, and the exact Markdown format that apply_structure parses. Pass feedback to be given the revision brief instead of the design brief - a revision must reproduce every unaffected title character for character, because pages are matched by title. Design the outline from this brief and send it to apply_structure. Costs nothing: no model is called. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. feedback string The changes you want made to the existing outline. Omit to design one from scratch.

Replace the outline writes destructiveReplaces a course's outline with the Markdown you give it. Chapters and pages are matched by title: a page whose title is unchanged keeps its text and its details, a page with a new title starts empty, and a page that is no longer in the outline is deleted along with everything written on it. Always send the complete outline - anything left out is removed. Run preview_structure first when the Markdown did not come from get_structure_brief. If the outline would remove a page that has text on it, this refuses and names those pages unless confirm_removals is true, so an outline that only adds and renames applies in one call. Returns what was added, what was kept and what was removed. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. structure * string The complete outline in CourseForge's Markdown format, as described by get_structure_brief. confirm_removals boolean Set true only when you mean to delete written pages that this outline leaves out. Without it the call is refused and the pages at stake are named.

Have CourseForge design the outline writes destructive spends creditCourseForge calls the course's own model and designs a complete outline. Existing chapters and pages are matched by title, so a new outline over a course that has already been written would delete every page it does not name. When it would take a page that has text on it, the outline is handed back for you to look at instead of being applied, and applying it then costs nothing - so the model is never called twice over the same decision. Pass confirm_removals to have it applied whatever it removes. Pass feedback to revise the existing outline rather than design a new one. It blocks while the model works, which on a large course takes a minute or two. To design an outline without spending anything at all, use get_structure_brief and apply_structure instead. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. feedback string The changes you want made to the existing outline. Omit to design one from scratch. confirm_removals boolean Set true only when you mean to delete written pages the new outline leaves out. Without it the designed outline is returned unapplied and the pages at stake are named.

Have CourseForge plan what each page teaches writes spends creditEvery page in an outline can carry a scope: one line, indented under its title, naming what that page and no other page teaches. Every page brief carries every page's scope, which is how a page knows what the others cover and leaves it to them. Outlines designed now come with scopes; this fills them in for pages that have none - an older outline, pages added by hand - in one request to the course's outline model, and writes them into the stored outline. Pass all to plan every page afresh. No page text is touched. To plan them without spending anything, add the scope lines to the outline yourself and store it with apply_structure. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. all boolean Plan every page afresh instead of only the pages that have no scope.

Read the outline readsThe stored outline of a course exactly as it is, plus what CourseForge reads out of it: the book title and description, how many chapters and pages there are, and every title. Read this before revising an outline, so that the titles you mean to keep stay byte-identical and their pages keep their text. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.

Check outline Markdown before applying it readsParses outline Markdown and reports what CourseForge understood from it - the book title, the description, every chapter with its pages, and any {{Tag}} markers - without touching any course. It takes no course_id and changes nothing. Use it whenever an outline was assembled by hand, because apply_structure deletes every page the outline leaves out and there is no undo. Reports duplicate titles, chapters with no pages and anything the parser could not read. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description structure * string The outline Markdown to check.

List and read pages, take a writing brief, store a finished page, and generate one through the profile's model. Also retitles pages and chapters and rewrites a chapter description, which edits the stored outline, because chapters and pages are matched by title.

Get the writing brief for a page readsThe complete writing brief for one page: the system instructions and the user prompt CourseForge would send a model, the content details resolved for it, and the shared course context - the course map, in which every page carries the scope it alone teaches, plus the chapter it belongs to. Write the page from this brief and send the result to write_page. Omit page_id to be given the next page that has not been written yet. The shared context is the same for page after page: pass the ids you were given back as known_context, and while they still match that text is left out of the answer instead of being sent again. Costs nothing: no model is called. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. page_id integer A specific page. Omit for the next unwritten one. feedback string Revision instructions, when rewriting a page that already has text. known_context string The shared_context_id and chapter_context_id you already hold from earlier briefs of this course, comma-separated. A segment whose id is listed is not repeated; one that has changed since - an edited outline, the next chapter - is sent again under a new id.

Store a written page writesStores the Markdown of one page. The text must follow the brief: GitHub-flavoured Markdown, no level-1 heading, no raw HTML. Returns how many pages are still unwritten, so a loop of brief - write - store knows when it is finished. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. page_id * integer The page this text belongs to. content * string The finished page, in Markdown.

List the pages of a course readsEvery page of a course in reading order, with its chapter, status, word count and whether it has been published. Lighter than get_course when all you need is what to write next. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. only string Which pages to return. One of all, written, unwritten, failed, unpublished.

Read one page readsOne page in full: its title, its Markdown, its extra context, its status and where it sits in the course. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. page_id * integer The page to read.

Edit a page writesChanges a page's title, its scope, its Markdown, or the extra context that is added to its brief the next time it is written. Only the fields you give are changed. A new title or scope also rewrites the stored outline, because both are lines of it and chapters and pages are matched by title. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. page_id * integer The page to change. title string A new title. scope string What this page and no other page teaches, as one line - concepts separated by semicolons. Every page brief shows every page's scope. An empty string removes it. content string New Markdown for the page. extra_context string Notes that are added to this page's brief - things this page in particular must cover, or must not. They are instructions to the writer, not text that appears on the page.

Edit a chapter writesChanges a chapter's title or its description. Renaming a chapter rewrites the stored outline, because chapters are matched by title. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. chapter_id * integer The chapter to change. title string A new title. description string A new description. This is part of what the pages are written from.

Have CourseForge write a page writes spends creditCourseForge calls the course's own model and writes one page, start to finish, and stores it. This is the opposite of get_page_brief: the work happens on the server and is billed to the profile's AI account. It blocks until the page is finished, which on a long page can take minutes - to write a whole course, use start_run instead. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. page_id integer The page to write. Omit for the next unwritten one. feedback string Revision instructions, when rewriting a page that already has text. extra_context string Notes to store on the page and add to its brief before writing it - things this page in particular must cover, or must not. Saved with the page, so a later rewrite carries them too. Omit to leave whatever the page already holds; update_page sets it without spending anything.

Correct the punctuation of what is already written writes destructiveSets the quotation marks, apostrophes, ellipses, dashes and spacing of a course, one chapter or one page the way the course language sets them - German gets „ and “ where the model wrote " and ", French gets its guillemets and its narrow spaces, an ellipsis becomes one character and a hyphen between two words becomes a dash. Code, links, formulas, HTML and anything the author escaped are never touched. Costs nothing: no model is called, the rules are all in code. page_id wins over chapter_id, which wins over the course, so course_id alone corrects the whole course. Send preview to be told what would change without changing it. Running it twice changes nothing the second time. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. chapter_id integer One chapter and its pages. Omit for the whole course. page_id integer One page. Omit for the whole chapter or course. language string Set the text as this language instead of the course's own. preview boolean Report what would change and write nothing.
The thirteen switchable elements and seven values, at course, chapter or page level.

List every content detail readsEvery content detail this installation has, with what it does and its installation-wide default: the switchable features - summary, exercises, diagrams, formulas, flashcards, code examples, tables, callouts, emojis, auto links and the rest - and the values such as minimum and maximum length, diagram count, card count and audience. This is the only place the valid keys, the value types and the permitted ranges are listed, so read it before calling set_details. Takes no arguments and costs nothing. No arguments.

Read the content details of one level readsWhat the content details are at one level and where each of them comes from. Give course_id alone for the course, add chapter_id for one chapter, or page_id for one page - page_id wins over chapter_id, which wins over the course. Every detail is reported three ways: what this level stores of its own, what it would inherit if it stored nothing, and what actually applies to a page written here. The chain is installation default, then the course's profile (see set_profile_details), then course, chapter, page. Features are tri-state, so a stored 0 means inherited, never off. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. chapter_id integer Read one chapter's level instead of the course's. page_id integer Read one page's level. Takes precedence over chapter_id.

List every content detail a course overrides readsEvery chapter and page of one course that stores a detail of its own, and what it stores - the whole of what the Details tab calls "overrides below the course", in one call. get_details answers for one level and says nothing about the rest, so finding the three pages in a fifty-page course that were given exercises meant fifty calls. Levels that inherit everything are left out, because inheriting is the ordinary case and listing it would bury the answer. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.

Set content details at one level writesSets content detail overrides on the course, on one chapter or on one page. The ids choose the level: page_id wins over chapter_id, which wins over the course, so course_id alone changes the whole course. features is an object keyed by feature - 1 or true switches it on, -1 or false switches it off, 0 or null removes the override so that level inherits again. values is an object keyed by value - a number or a string sets it, null clears it back to inherited. Only the keys you send are touched; everything else stays as it was. Keys are checked against get_detail_catalogue and a wrong one is rejected with the list of valid ones. Returns the resolved details afterwards so you can see the effect. This changes what the next generation writes and never edits a page that already has text. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. chapter_id integer Set the override on one chapter instead of the course. page_id integer Set the override on one page. Takes precedence over chapter_id. features object Feature keys mapped to 1 / true (on), -1 / false (off) or 0 / null (inherit). For example {"exercises": 1, "emojis": -1, "mermaid": 0}. values object Value keys mapped to a number, a string, or null to inherit. For example {"min_length": 800, "diagram_max": 1, "audience": "experienced developers"}.

Clear the content details of one level writes destructiveRemoves every content detail override at one level so it inherits everything again: a page falls back to its chapter, a chapter to its course, and the course to the installation defaults. The ids choose the level the same way as set_details - page_id wins over chapter_id, which wins over the course. Nothing else is touched: resetting a chapter leaves its pages' own overrides in place. The cleared overrides are returned, so the same set_details call can put them back if this was a mistake. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. chapter_id integer Clear one chapter's overrides instead of the course's. page_id integer Clear one page's overrides. Takes precedence over chapter_id.
The tag library and what is tagged with what.

List the tag library readsOne account's tag library: every tag with its name, its value, and how many courses, chapters and pages it is attached to. Tags belong to an account, not to a course, so the same tag is reused everywhere. An administrator sees every account's tags, each marked with its owner - a library stays your own unless you widen it. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description owner string Administrators only: one other account's library. all boolean Administrators only: widen to every account on the installation. Without it a listing is your own.

Add a tag to the library writesAdds a tag to your library. It is attached to nothing yet, so this is only worth calling when you want the tag to exist before it is used - attach_tag creates a missing tag itself. A name already in the library is refused; change that one with update_tag instead. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description name * string The tag name, as it will appear in BookStack. value string The tag value. BookStack shows a tag as "name: value"; leave it out for a bare label.

Rename or revalue a tag writesChanges a tag's name or value in the library, which changes it everywhere it is attached at once. Anything already in BookStack keeps the old tag until that course is pushed again, so follow this with publish_course for any course that is live. Only the fields you give are changed. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description tag_id * integer The tag to change, as returned by list_tags. name string A new name. value string A new value. Send an empty string to clear it.

Delete a tag writes destructiveRemoves a tag from the library and from every course, chapter and page it is attached to. This cannot be undone, and it does not remove the tag from anything already published - push those courses again afterwards. Requires the tag name as confirmation. To stop one tag being published from one place without losing it everywhere, use set_tag_link with enabled false instead. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description tag_id * integer The tag to delete, as returned by list_tags. confirm_name * string The exact name of the tag, as a confirmation that the right one is being deleted.

Read every tag in a course readsEvery tag in play anywhere in one course: what is attached at the course, at each chapter and at each page, which of those inherit downwards, which CourseForge created itself from {{Tag}} markers in the outline, and which are switched off. Each item also carries its effective tags - what would actually be published for it, its own plus everything inherited from above. Items with no tags at all are left out. Costs nothing: no model is called. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.

Attach a tag writesAttaches a tag to the course, to one chapter or to one page, adding it to the owner's library first if it is not there yet. Set inherit to have it apply to everything below as well - from the course to every chapter and page, from a chapter to its own pages - which is how a course-wide tag is done without one link per page. Attaching by hand also turns an automatic tag into a manual one and switches it back on. Call publish_course afterwards to push the change to BookStack. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. name * string The tag name. A tag of this name is created if the library has none. value string The tag value. This is the value in the library, so setting it here changes the tag everywhere it is used. Leave it out to keep whatever the tag already has. target string What to attach it to: the whole course (the default), one chapter, or one page. One of course, project, chapter, page. target_id integer The chapter id or page id, when target is chapter or page. inherit boolean Also apply this tag to everything below the item. Ignored on a page, which has nothing below it.

Detach a tag writesRemoves one link between a tag and a course, chapter or page. The tag stays in the library and stays attached to everything else. A tag CourseForge created from a {{Tag}} marker comes back the next time the outline is generated, so for one of those use set_tag_link with enabled false - that decision is kept. Name the tag with exactly one of tag_id and name, whichever you have to hand. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. tag_id integer The tag to detach, as returned by get_course_tags. Give this or name, and not both. name string The tag to detach, by name, looked up in the library of the account that owns the course - the same name attach_tag takes. Give this or tag_id, and not both. target string Where to detach it from: the whole course (the default), one chapter, or one page. One of course, project, chapter, page. target_id integer The chapter id or page id, when target is chapter or page.

Change how a tag is attached writesChanges an existing link without removing it: whether it inherits downwards, and whether it is switched on. A switched-off link is kept but ignored everywhere - it reaches no writing brief and no BookStack push - which is how an automatic tag is stopped from being published without deleting it, and unlike a detach it survives a regenerated outline. Give at least one of inherit and enabled. The tag has to be attached to that item already; use attach_tag if it is not. Name the tag with exactly one of tag_id and name, whichever you have to hand. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. tag_id integer The tag whose link is being changed, as returned by get_course_tags. Give this or name, and not both. name string The tag whose link is being changed, by name, looked up in the library of the account that owns the course. Give this or tag_id, and not both. target string Which link: the one on the course (the default), on one chapter, or on one page. One of course, project, chapter, page. target_id integer The chapter id or page id, when target is chapter or page. inherit boolean Whether the tag also applies to everything below. Cannot be set on a page. enabled boolean Whether the link counts at all. False keeps it but hides it from every brief and every push.
Start, watch and cancel background and batch runs. This is the group that spends money at scale.

Write pages on the server writes spends creditStarts writing a set of pages on the server, and returns at once. The run is recorded before any work begins, so it carries on after this client disconnects, after the session ends and across a restart of the server - start it, go away, and call poll_run or list_runs later to see where it got to. A live run is written by CourseForge's own scheduler in the background and therefore needs cron to be configured: when it is not, this tool starts nothing and says so, and the ways round it are to have an administrator set app.cron_token, to switch to a batch run, or to write pages one at a time with generate_page. A batch run hands the whole selection to the provider's own queue at roughly half the price and is answered within 24 hours, which is the right choice for a large course where time is not critical. mode auto reads the profile's page model: a model ending in ":batch" queues, anything else goes to the background worker. Call estimate_run first to see the size of it. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. pages any Which pages to write. Omit it, or "unwritten", for every page that has no text yet - the usual case. "all" rewrites the whole course, pages that are already written included. "failed" retries the ones whose last attempt errored. Or give a list of page ids from list_pages. Pages already claimed by another run are left out of the keyword selections. chapter_id integer Restrict the run to one chapter. It combines with pages: the selection is then made inside that chapter

What a run would cost readsWhat start_run would do with the same arguments, without doing it and without spending anything: how many pages, which model and provider, whether it would go to the background worker or to the batch queue, and roughly how many input and output tokens are involved. The input figure is measured from the real prompts - the same ones the run would send - sampled across the selection and scaled up, and the answer says how many pages were measured and at how many characters to the token. No price is given: CourseForge does not know what an account pays, and a confident number in the wrong currency is worse than a token count. Read the warnings: the usual one is that the provider has a batch queue nobody is using. The prompts it measures are built and thrown away and no model is ever called, so finding out what a run would cost is itself free. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. pages any Which pages to write. Omit it, or "unwritten", for every page that has no text yet - the usual case. "all" rewrites the whole course, pages that are already written included. "failed" retries the ones whose last attempt errored. Or give a list of page ids from list_pages. Pages already claimed by another run are left out of the keyword selections. chapter_id integer Restrict the estimate to one chapter. mode string Which way to cost it. auto reads the profile's page model, as start_run would. One of auto, live, batch.

List generation runs readsEvery run this account can see, newest first, with the course it belongs to, whether it is live or batch, its status, and how many of its pages are written, still pending, skipped or failed. This is the tool to call after reconnecting, to find out whether work ordered earlier is still going. only=open lists just the runs that have not ended; all and finished look at the 100 newest. Follow with get_run for the detail of one, or poll_run to make a batch check in now. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id integer One course only. Omit for every course this account can see. only string Which runs to return. open means anything that has not ended. One of all, open, finished.

Read one run readsOne run in detail: its status, its mode, the model and provider behind it, the page counts, when it started, when it was last checked, and - for a batch - the provider's own id and the moment its results expire and stop being collectable. include_items adds every page in the run with its own status and error message, which is how you find out which three of five hundred pages failed and why. This reads what is stored and asks the provider nothing; poll_run is the one that goes out to the network. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description run_id * integer The run, as returned by list_runs or start_run. include_items boolean Include every page in the run with its own status and error. On a large run this is a long list.

Check a run now writesAsks the provider now whether a batch has finished, and writes home every page that has, instead of waiting for the next scheduler tick to do it. Use it when you want the answer in this conversation. On a live run there is no provider to ask: it reports where the background worker has got to and closes the run if the last page has landed. Safe to call as often as you like - the same page is never written twice - and it spends nothing beyond what the run has already committed. It reports how many pages arrived since the previous check. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description run_id * integer The run to check.

Stop a run writes destructiveStops a run and releases the pages it was holding back to unwritten. At the provider it is best effort: a batch that has already finished cannot be cancelled, and is collected and written home instead of being thrown away. A page a live worker is writing at this very moment is left to finish, because it has already been paid for. Pages that were written before the cancel stay written - this stops the work, it does not undo it. Use delete_run afterwards to remove the record. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description run_id * integer The run to stop.

Forget a finished run writes destructiveRemoves the record of a run that has ended. This is bookkeeping only: every page the run wrote stays exactly as it is, and nothing is refunded or recalled. A run that is still open is refused - stop it with cancel_run first, then delete it. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description run_id * integer The finished run to forget.

Is anything collecting background work readsWhether background work will actually be picked up on this installation: whether a cron token is configured, when the scheduler last called in, how many worker slots it has, and how many runs and pages are waiting for it. Ask before starting a live run if you want to be sure something will collect it, because a background run on an installation with no scheduler sits untouched for ever. A batch run can be submitted without the scheduler - the provider holds that work - but then its results have to be collected with poll_run. Costs nothing. No arguments.
AI accounts, models and BookStack instances. Keys are never readable, but they can be replaced.

List profiles readsThe profiles this account can generate with: the id to pass to update_course, the AI accounts each one holds and what kind they are, whether each account has a key stored, the models chosen for the outline and the page slot, the BookStack instances, and the language. API keys are never included - only whether one is set. An administrator sees every account's profiles, each marked with its owner - a working set stays your own unless you widen it. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description owner string Administrators only: one other account's profiles. all boolean Administrators only: widen to every account on the installation. Without it a listing is your own.

Read a profile readsOne profile in full: every AI account with its kind, base URL and whether a key is stored, every BookStack instance, both model slots with their temperature and token ceiling, the language, the concurrency, the courses using it, and the prompt slots this profile overrides - so you can see how it differs from the installation defaults. No credential is ever returned. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile id, as returned by list_profiles. include_prompt_text boolean Include the full text of each prompt override rather than only which slots are overridden. These can be long.

Create a profile writesBuilds a working profile in one call: one AI account, both model slots pointed at it, the language, and optionally a BookStack instance. Call list_providers first to see which account kinds this installation speaks and which of them need a key. The key is stored on the server and can never be read back - only replaced. The profile belongs to the account that creates it. Follow with check_profile to prove the credentials work and list_models to choose a model. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description name * string A short name for the profile, for the picker. ai_kind string The kind of AI account. Call list_providers for what each one is and whether it needs a key. One of openai, anthropic, gemini, openrouter, oai-compat. api_key string The API key for the account. Required for every kind whose needs_key is true. Written only: no tool will ever hand it back. base_url string The endpoint. Omit to use the default list_providers gives for this kind, which is right for everything but a self-hosted or proxied gateway. preset_key string A row of the provider catalogue rather than a raw driver kind - "groq", "together", "deepseek", "llamacpp" and the rest, as list_providers reports them. Naming one picks the endpoint and the label with it, which is what the browser's provider picker does; ai_kind is then optional. Every preset runs on the OpenAI-compatible driver. organization string The OpenAI organization id, for an account that belongs to one. site_url string OpenRouter only: the site this traffic is attributed to. site_name string OpenRouter only: the nam

Change a profile writesChanges one profile. Only the fields you give are touched, and everything else - the other accounts, the prompt overrides - is left exactly as it was. An omitted or empty api_key keeps the stored key: passing "" does not clear it, and there is no way to blank a stored key at all, so an account whose key must go has to be replaced with a new one or the profile deleted and made again. Give ai_id when the profile holds more than one AI account, and bookstack_id when it holds more than one instance. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to change. name string A new name for the profile. ai_id string Which AI account to change, when the profile holds more than one. get_profile lists the ids. ai_name string A new name for that AI account, for the picker. ai_kind string Change the account to another kind. The base URL follows the new kind's default unless you gave one yourself or had typed one. One of openai, anthropic, gemini, openrouter, oai-compat. api_key string A new key, replacing the stored one. Empty or omitted keeps what is stored. base_url string A new endpoint for the account. preset_key string A row of the provider catalogue rather than a raw driver kind - "groq", "together", "deepseek", "llamacpp" and the rest, as list_providers reports them. Naming one picks the endpoint and the label with it, which is what the browser's provider picker does; ai_kind is then optional. Every preset runs on the OpenAI-compatible driver. organization string The OpenAI organization id, for an account that belongs to one. site_url

Delete a profile writes destructiveRemoves a profile and the credentials in it. The keys are gone and cannot be recovered, because nothing here can read them back to copy them elsewhere first. A profile a course still points at is refused, with the names of the courses - move them to another profile with update_course before deleting this one. Requires the profile name as confirmation. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to delete. confirm_name * string The exact name of the profile, as a confirmation that the right one is being deleted.

Add an AI account to a profile writesAdds another AI account to a profile that already has one - an OpenAI key beside an Anthropic one, a self-hosted gateway beside both, the Claude subscription beside a metered key. update_profile changes an account a profile already holds; this is how it gets a second. Call list_providers first for the kinds this installation speaks. Nothing points at the new account until you say so: use set_model_slot to send the outline or the pages through it. The key is stored on the server and can never be read back. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to add the account to. kind string The kind of AI account. Call list_providers for what each one is and whether it needs a key. One of openai, anthropic, gemini, openrouter, oai-compat. name string A name for this account, which is how the model slots refer to it. Defaults to the provider's own label. api_key string The API key. Required for every kind whose needs_key is true. Written only: no tool will ever hand it back. base_url string The endpoint. Omit to use the default list_providers gives for this kind. preset_key string A row of the provider catalogue rather than a raw driver kind - "groq", "together", "deepseek", "llamacpp" and the rest, as list_providers reports them. Naming one picks the endpoint and the label with it, which is what the browser's provider picker does; ai_kind is then optional. Every preset runs on the OpenAI-compatible driver. organization string The OpenAI organization id, for an account that belongs to one. site_url string OpenRouter

Remove an AI account from a profile writes destructiveTakes one AI account out of a profile. Its key goes with it and cannot be recovered, because nothing here can read a key back to copy it elsewhere first. A model slot pointing at the account is left pointing at nothing, which stops that slot generating until it is pointed somewhere with set_model_slot - so the answer says which slots those were. Removing the last account of a profile is refused: a profile with no account cannot write a word, and deleting the profile is the honest way to say that. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile the account belongs to. ai_id * string The account to remove. get_profile lists the ids.

Add a BookStack instance to a profile writesAdds another BookStack instance to a profile that already has one - a staging wiki beside a live one, the wikis of two departments, a customer's install beside your own. update_profile changes an instance a profile already holds; this is how it gets a second, which is what a course needs before set_publish_targets can send it to more than one wiki. The token secret is stored on the server and can never be read back. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to add the instance to. url * string The BookStack base URL, without a trailing slash. token_id * string The BookStack API token id. Not a secret; it is readable back. token_secret * string The BookStack API token secret. Written only: no tool will ever hand it back. name string A name for this instance, which is how a course names its destination. bookstackdev_id integer The BookStackDev look this instance should wear, by id. Omit for plain BookStack.

Remove a BookStack instance from a profile writes destructiveTakes one BookStack instance out of a profile, with its token. A course that publishes to that instance loses the destination and the record of the book it made there, so publishing to the same wiki later would create a second book beside the first - the call is refused with the names of those courses unless you send confirm. Nothing is deleted inside BookStack itself, here or ever. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile the instance belongs to. bookstack_id * string The instance to remove. get_profile lists the ids. confirm boolean Go through with it even though courses publish to this instance. Their destinations and the record of what was published there are forgotten.

Point one model slot at an account and a model writesSets the outline slot or the page slot on its own: which AI account it runs through, which model, and that slot's own temperature and token ceiling. update_profile sets both slots together, which is right when a profile has one account and wrong as soon as it has two - the outline is one call and can afford the expensive model, while the pages are hundreds and may want a cheaper one, a different provider, or ":batch" on the end to go through the provider's queue at about half price. Call list_models for the ids an account will accept. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to change. slot * string Which slot: "outline" designs the course structure, "page" writes the pages. One of outline, page. model string The model id, as list_models reports it. Add ":batch" to route this slot through the provider's queue. ai_id string The AI account this slot runs through. Omit to leave it where it points, or when the profile holds only one account. temperature number Sampling temperature for this slot alone. 0.7 unless you have a reason. max_tokens integer The token ceiling for one reply from this slot. 0 means the provider's own default.

List the prompt slots a profile can override readsEvery prompt slot this installation has: its key, the group it belongs to, what it is for, the placeholders it may use, and the wording currently in force for the installation - which is what a profile that overrides nothing uses. This is the read a profile needs before set_profile_prompts can change one, and unlike get_prompts it needs no administrator, because overriding a slot for one profile is not the same power as rewriting it for everybody. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description group string One group only, as the group field of a slot reports it. include_text boolean Include the full wording of each slot rather than only what it is for. These are long.

Override prompt slots for one profile writesReplaces the wording this profile uses for one or more prompt slots, leaving the installation's own prompts alone for every other profile. This is the per-profile half of get_prompts and set_prompts, which are the installation-wide pair and need an administrator: a profile override needs only the profile. Call get_prompts for the slot names and what each one is for, and get_profile with include_prompt_text to read back what this profile currently overrides. A slot named in reset goes back to the installation's wording; an empty string is a deliberate override that sends nothing for that slot, which is not the same thing. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to change. prompts object Slot name to the text this profile should use instead. Unknown slot names are refused rather than silently stored. reset array Slot names to stop overriding, so the installation's wording applies again.

Set the content defaults of one profile writesDecides content details for every course written with this profile - which elements a page gets and the values that size them - one level above the course. The chain is: installation default, then this profile, then course, chapter, page, the closest level winning. A course inherits whatever the profile decides until it overrides it, so this is where a house style lives: "every course on this profile opens with learning objectives and aims at 1,500 words". Call get_detail_catalogue for the keys, the types and the ranges. features maps a key to 1 (on), -1 (off) or 0 (stop deciding, so the installation default applies again); values maps a key to a number or a piece of text, or null to stop deciding. reset_all drops everything this profile decided. Nothing already written changes - the next page generated on any course of this profile follows the new answer. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile to change. features object Feature key to 1 (on), -1 (off) or 0 (inherit the installation default). Unknown keys are refused rather than silently dropped. values object Value key to the number or text this profile decides, or null to stop deciding it. Numbers are clamped to the range get_detail_catalogue reports. reset_all boolean Drop every content detail this profile decided, so its courses follow the installation defaults again. Can be combined with features and values, which are applied afterwards.

List the models an account can use readsAsks the provider which models this account may actually call, and marks which of them its batch queue accepts. Writing a model as "claude-opus-5:batch" in a profile routes the whole course through that queue at about half the price, at the cost of waiting - up to a day for the answer, which is why the suffix belongs on the page slot and not on the outline. An empty batch list means the provider would not say, not that nothing can be queued: supports_batch is the answer then. This is a live call to the provider and can take a few seconds, but no provider charges for a model listing. Pass the chosen id back to update_profile as model or structure_model. Reaches the provider but buys nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile the account belongs to. ai_id string Which AI account to ask, when the profile holds more than one. refresh boolean Accepted and ignored: the list is fetched from the provider on every call, so it is never stale.

Check that an account works writesAnswers "does this account work" before a whole course depends on it, by making one live call and reporting what came back.
