For a key-based account that call is a model listing, which is the cheapest thing that proves the base URL and the key are both right, and no provider bills for it; for the Claude subscription account, which has no model listing to fetch, it reports whether the CLI is installed, whether it is signed in, and whether an API key in the server environment has quietly taken over the billing. Use list_models when the question is which models to choose rather than whether the credentials are good. Reaches the provider but buys nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile the account belongs to. ai_id string Which AI account to check, when the profile holds more than one.

List the account kinds readsEvery kind of AI account this installation can speak: its key for ai_kind, its label, the base URL it defaults to, whether it needs an API key, whether it has a batch queue, and a line of guidance on what belongs there. Call this before create_profile - the catalogue is what create_profile validates ai_kind against, and it grows. Read from this installation, so nothing is contacted. Costs nothing. No arguments.

List BookStack shelves readsThe shelves the profile's BookStack instance offers, with their ids, so a course can be filed onto one when it is published. This is a network call to the BookStack server and also proves the token works. A course carries the shelf on its own publishing settings, not on the profile: pass the id you choose to update_course as shelf_id, with the name as shelf_name. Reaches the BookStack server but buys nothing. Argument Type Description profile_id * integer The profile the instance belongs to. bookstack_id string Which BookStack instance to ask, when the profile holds more than one. get_profile lists the ids.

List BookStackDev looks readsThe looks this account has made for its BookStack instances: name, which instances wear it, which other addresses the link is allowed on, and the embed line. A look is a BookStackDev configuration - Shiki code highlighting, Mermaid, MathJax, link embeds, an audio player, external-link marks, a light/dark button, page styling - served to a wiki by one script tag. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description owner string Administrators only: the account whose looks to list. all boolean Administrators only: every account's looks.

What a look can be told readsEvery option a BookStackDev look has, grouped by feature, with its type, its default and its range - the keys create_bookstackdev_profile and update_bookstackdev_profile take in settings. Also the Shiki themes the code highlighter knows. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Read one look readsOne look in full: every setting, the instances wearing it, every address the link works on, the embed line for a wiki's custom head, and the conventions check - whether the prompts of the profiles publishing into it agree with what it renders. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description bookstackdev_id * integer The look, as returned by list_bookstackdev_profiles.

Create a look writesMakes a look with every feature switched on the way the shipped BookStackDev is, changed by whatever settings you give. Name the BookStack instances that should wear it (get_profile lists their ids) and any other address the link should work on - a wiki CourseForge holds no credentials for. The answer carries the embed line. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description name * string What to call it, for the picker. settings object Settings to change from the defaults, keyed by group then field - see list_bookstackdev_options. {"codeBlocks": {"themeDark": "github-dark"}} instance_ids array BookStack instance ids, from get_profile, that wear this look. origins array Other addresses the link may be loaded on, as origins: https://wiki.example.com. The instances above are allowed without being listed here.

Change a look writesChanges one look. Only what you give is touched: a settings object changes the fields it names and no other, instance_ids replaces the list of instances wearing it, origins replaces the list of extra addresses. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description bookstackdev_id * integer The look to change. name string A new name. settings object Fields to change, keyed by group then field - see list_bookstackdev_options. instance_ids array The complete list of instance ids that wear this look afterwards. origins array The complete list of extra origins afterwards.

Delete a look writes destructiveRemoves a look. Its link stops answering at once, and every instance wearing it goes back to plain BookStack. Requires the name as confirmation. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description bookstackdev_id * integer The look to delete. confirm_name * string The exact name of the look, as a confirmation that the right one is being deleted.

Regenerate the link of a look writes destructiveGives a look a new key, and so a new embed line. The old line is refused from this moment wherever it was pasted, which is how a link that got copied somewhere it should not have been is taken back. Every wiki using it has to paste the new line. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description bookstackdev_id * integer The look whose link to regenerate.

Check a look against the prompts readsWhether the prompts of every profile publishing into an instance wearing this look agree with what the look renders: formulas written for delimiters it does not typeset, diagrams or formulas asked for while the feature is off. A finding about a prompt carries the recommended wording, which set_profile_prompts can write. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description bookstackdev_id * integer The look to check.
Push a course into BookStack and resolve cross references.

What has been published readsThe publishing state of one course, worked out from CourseForge's own records without contacting BookStack: every BookStack instance the course publishes to with its shelf, its book and how much of the course is in each of them, how many chapters and pages are in sync, how many have changed since the last push, how many have never been pushed, how many pages have no text to push yet, and how many cross-reference markers would still fail to become links. A course may publish to several instances at once; the counts are folded across the ones that are switched on, so "in sync" means in sync everywhere and "changed" means at least one of them would be written to. Read this before publish_course to see what a push would do. It is counts and a summary rather than a list, so it stays small whatever the size of the course, and it changes nothing. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.

Publish to BookStack writes destructivePushes the course into every BookStack instance the course points at. For each of them it creates the book if it is not there yet, puts it on that instance's chosen shelf, then creates or updates every chapter and every page, carrying the effective tags with them. Items that have not changed since the last push to that instance are skipped and an item that was deleted there is recreated, so re-publishing never duplicates anything. Pages with no text yet are skipped. Each instance holds its own book with its own ids, and a page's cross references point inside the wiki it is in, so the same page is written slightly differently to each. An instance that cannot be reached does not stop the others: its failure is reported and the push carries on. This is a long sequence of API calls against somebody else's live wiki, times the number of instances, and can take several minutes on a large course; existing chapters and pages are overwritten in place, and none of it can be undone from CourseForge. part "all" publishes the whole course and resolves cross references afterwards; part "chapter" or "page" publishes one item and needs target_id, creates the book and the parent chapter around it, and leaves cross references alone - call resolve_links after those. force re-sends items whose fingerprint says they are unchanged, which also overwrites edits made in BookStack by hand. The course has to say where it publishes first: set_publish_targets sets the whole list, and update_course still sets a single one as bookstack_instance. No model is called -

Turn cross references into links writesRewrites the ( 🔗 Title ) markers the writer left in the text into real BookStack links, using the URLs of what has already been published, and re-sends only the pages whose text actually changed. It calls no model and can be run as often as you like - the stored page always keeps the raw marker, so resolving is repeatable and never corrupts the source text. A reference whose target is not published yet keeps its marker and resolves on a later run; a reference that matches no chapter or page in the course goes out as plain text, and list_unresolved_links says which ones those are. A full publish_course already does this, so run it after publishing a single chapter or page, or after a page was rewritten. Each rewritten page is written back to the live wiki - this reaches the BookStack server but buys nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. instances array Resolve into these BookStack instances only, named by their instance id. Leave it out for every instance the course has switched on. Each wiki gets links pointing inside itself. force boolean Re-send every page that holds a marker, even one whose text has not changed.

Where a course publishes writes destructiveSets the whole list of BookStack instances a course publishes to, in one call. A course may have several: the same book written into a staging wiki and a live one, or into the wikis of two departments. Each entry names an instance the course's profile defines - list_profiles shows them - and may carry a shelf and a switch. The first entry is the one the course reports as its own book and shelf everywhere a single answer is wanted. An entry left off the list is forgotten together with the record of what was published into it, so the next push there creates a second book rather than updating the first: to stop publishing to a wiki without losing that record, send it with enabled false instead. Nothing here reaches BookStack and nothing already published is changed or deleted - this only says where the next push goes. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. targets * array Every instance this course publishes to, in order. An empty list means the course publishes nowhere, which clears its book and shelf.

Cross references that will not become links readsEvery cross-reference marker that does not turn into a link, and the page it sits on. Two kinds: markers whose title matches no chapter or page in this course, each with the closest existing title as a suggestion - those go out as plain text and are the ones people never notice - and markers whose target does exist but has not been published yet, which resolve by themselves once it is. This is what to check after a publish. It lists one row per affected page, so on a large course with many cross references the answer is long. Reads the stored text only: no model, no BookStack, nothing changed. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses.
Who you are connected as, your own password and display name, and your own connections. Never anybody else's.

Who am I connected as readsThe account this connection belongs to, its role, and what this installation of CourseForge can currently do - whether the scheduler is running, so background runs are possible, and how many courses the account can see. No arguments.

Read my account readsEverything this installation records about the account this connection belongs to - its user name, display name, role, when it was made and when it last signed in - together with every MCP connection it owns and the tool groups each of those carries. Passwords are stored only as hashes and tokens only as digests, so neither appears here. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Rename myself writesChanges the name shown for this account in the interface and against its courses. The user name is the key everything is filed under and cannot be changed; this is only the friendly name beside it. An empty value falls back to the user name. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description display_name * string The name to show for this account.

Change my password writesSets a new password for this account. The current one has to be given and has to be right, so a connection that has been handed round cannot lock the owner out of their own installation. A password needs at least 10 characters and has to differ from the current one. This does not sign anything out and does not revoke any connection: open browser sessions and every MCP connection, this one included, carry on working. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description current_password * string The password this account has now. Ask the person for it rather than guessing - a wrong value changes nothing and is refused. new_password * string The password to set, at least 10 characters. Leading and trailing spaces are kept, because they are part of a password.

List my MCP connections readsThe MCP connections this account owns: the name each was given, the tool groups it is limited to, when it was made, when it was last used, how often, and whether it still works. Two things stop one working without removing it - passing its expiry date, and being older than the last password an administrator set for this account. Only connections belonging to this account are ever listed, whatever its role. Tokens are stored as hashes and can never be shown again. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Revoke one of my connections writes destructiveDeletes the token of one connection belonging to this account, so the next request it makes is refused. Revoking the connection you are talking through ends this conversation immediately and no further tool call will work - and this tool cannot tell you whether that is the one, because a handler is told which account is calling and never which connection. Call list_my_connections first and match the name against the client you are running in. This cannot be undone: a replacement has to be made from the Connect screen in the browser. Requires the connection name as confirmation. Argument Type Description connection_id * integer The connection to revoke, as returned by list_my_connections. confirm_name * string The exact name of that connection, as a confirmation that the right one is being cut off.

List the tool groups a connection can be limited to readsEvery tool group this installation has: its key, what it covers, whether it needs an administrator and whether anything in it spends money on the AI account. It also says which groups this account may hold at all, and which the connection you are talking through holds right now - which is the ceiling on what create_my_connection will issue. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Issue a new MCP connection for this account writesMints a token for another Claude client to connect with, in this account's name - the same thing the Connect screen does, for setting a second machine up without opening a browser. The token is returned exactly once and is never recoverable: the database keeps only a hash. A new connection may hold no tool group that the connection asking for it does not already hold, so a narrowed token can copy itself or make something smaller and never something larger; naming a group this connection lacks is refused rather than quietly dropped. Leaving scopes out means the same groups this connection has. Call list_scopes for the keys. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description name * string What to call the connection, so it is recognisable in the list. scopes array Tool groups the new connection may use, by key. Omit for the same groups this connection holds. ttl_days integer Days until it expires by itself. 0 means it never does, which is what the browser offers by default. note string A line about which machine it is for, shown beside it in the list.

Rename one of my connections writesChanges the name or the note on a connection belonging to this account. Only those two: the tool groups and the expiry are what the token was issued to do, and widening them afterwards would make the record of what was issued a lie - to change either, revoke it and issue another. An omitted field keeps what is stored. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description connection_id * integer The connection to rename, as returned by list_my_connections. name string A new name. note string A new note.
Accounts, settings, the cron token, diagnostics and updates. Only ever available to an administrator. Administrators only.

Hand a course to another account writes adminAdministrators only. Moves a course to another account. Its profile belongs to the old owner and will not resolve for the new one, so the assignment is cleared and has to be made again. Argument Type Description course_id * integer The course id, as returned by list_courses. to * string The user name of the account that should own the course.

List accounts reads adminEvery account on this installation: user name, role, whether it is disabled, when it last signed in, and how much it owns - courses, pages, profiles, tags and connections. Read this before changing or deleting an account, because those content counts are what a deletion is actually about. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Create an account writes adminCreates an account. Leave password out and CourseForge generates one and returns it in this answer exactly once - only a hash is stored, so it cannot be read again afterwards. The account is asked to choose its own password at the first sign-in unless must_change_password is false. To let somebody create their own account instead of being handed a password, use issue_invite. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description username * string The user name to sign in with. Letters, digits, spaces and . _ @ + - are allowed. role string user owns its own courses and nothing else. admin can also manage accounts, settings and updates. Defaults to user. One of user, admin. password string A password of at least 10 characters. Omit it to have one generated and returned here. display_name string The name shown in the interface. Defaults to the user name. must_change_password boolean Ask this account to choose a new password at the first sign-in. Defaults to true.

Change an account writes adminChanges one account: its role, its display name, whether it is disabled, or its password. Only the fields you give are changed. Setting a password here replaces the old one without knowing it, and asks the account to choose a new one at the next sign-in. The last enabled administrator cannot be demoted or disabled, and this connection's own account cannot demote or disable itself. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description username * string The account to change, as returned by list_users. role string A new role. One of user, admin. display_name string A new display name. disabled boolean true refuses every sign-in and every connection token this account owns, without deleting anything. false lets it back in. password string A new password, of at least 10 characters. Setting one cuts off every MCP connection the account made before now, because a reset is how somebody who has held this password is cut off.

Delete an account writes destructive adminRemoves an account. content says what happens to everything it owns: "delete" destroys its courses, pages, profiles, tags and connections, and "transfer" hands them to transfer_to, or to you if that is left out. Deleted content cannot be recovered, so confirm_username has to match the account name exactly. Call list_users first to see how much is at stake. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description username * string The account to delete. content * string What happens to the courses, profiles, tags and connections this account owns. One of delete, transfer. transfer_to string The account that inherits the content when content is "transfer". Defaults to the account this connection belongs to. confirm_username * string The exact user name again, as a confirmation that the right account is being deleted.

Issue an invite code writes adminReturns a fresh invite code exactly once, so somebody can create their own account from the sign-in screen rather than being handed a password over a chat. The database keeps only a hash, so the code cannot be read back later - pass it on now. Several invites may be open at once, each with its own label, role, expiry and number of places; issuing one leaves the others alone. It is good for a single account unless max_uses says otherwise. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description role string The role the account created with this code gets. Defaults to user. One of user, admin. label string Who this invite is for - "marketing team", "the contractor" - so it can be told from the others in list_users and revoked by name. Up to 80 characters. ttl_hours integer How long the code stays valid. Defaults to 48 hours. max_uses integer How many accounts this one code may create. Defaults to 1. Anything above that is a code worth several accounts to whoever finds the file it is written in, so raise it only for a group you are expecting.

Revoke an open invite code writes destructive adminCancels an open invite, so the code stops working and nobody else can redeem it. list_users shows the open invites with their ids and labels; name one with invite_id, or leave it out to revoke the newest. Accounts already created from it keep working - revoking closes the door, it does not undo who came through. Refused when there is no open invite. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description invite_id integer The invite to revoke, from list_users. Omit for the newest open one.

Show the scheduler URL reads adminThe finished URL a scheduler calls to run background and batch work, built from the cron token this installation already has. generate_cron_token returns the same URL but makes a new token first, which stops every scheduler still calling the old one - so this is the tool for "what should I paste into cron", and that one is for "the secret has leaked". Refused when no token has been generated yet. Costs nothing. No arguments.

List settings reads adminEvery setting this installation has: key, label, description, type, the current value, the value the release ships, and whether this installation has overridden it. The value of a secret - the cron token, the GitHub token - is never returned; you are told only whether one is stored. Use the keys from here with set_settings. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description group string One group only: general, content, scheduler, batch, updates, mcp, security, timeouts. Omit for all of them.

Change settings writes adminWrites one or more settings. values is an object of setting key to new value, and every value is validated against the catalogue before anything is written, so one bad value changes nothing at all. An unknown key is refused and the valid ones are listed. An empty string for a secret leaves the stored secret alone rather than clearing it - reset_setting clears one. Call list_settings first for the keys, their types and their ranges. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description values * object Setting key to new value, for instance {"app.name": "Team CourseForge", "app.cron_workers": 4}.

Reset a setting writes adminDrops this installation's override for one setting, so the value the release ships applies again. Use it to undo a change without having to know what the default was. Resetting app.cron_token clears the cron secret and stops background runs until generate_cron_token makes a new one. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description key * string The setting to reset, as returned by list_settings.

Generate the cron token writes adminMakes a new cron secret, stores it, and returns the finished URL to paste into a hosting control panel as a job that runs once a minute. This URL is what makes background and batch runs possible at all: with no token, cron.php answers 404 to everybody and long runs are not offered. The token is returned here once and cannot be read back afterwards, and any scheduler still calling the old URL stops working the moment this returns - so only generate a new one when you are able to update the scheduler as well. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Measure PHP and raise what is too low writes adminReads the PHP configuration this host gives CourseForge, works out which limits are below what it needs, and writes a .user.ini raising exactly those. Every number is a floor and every run only ever raises: a directive already set is never removed or lowered, and a limit the host is generous about is left alone. Reports what it could not change, because some directives are fixed by the host and a line for them would be ignored in silence. Idempotent - running it twice writes nothing the second time. Pass dry_run to see the plan without touching anything at all. Pass release to take CourseForge's settings back out and let the host's own values return, which is what moving to different hosting wants. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description dry_run boolean Report what would happen, writing and storing nothing. release boolean Remove CourseForge's block from .user.ini and let this host's own values return. They come back once PHP re-reads the file, which takes up to user_ini.cache_ttl seconds.

Run the installation check reads adminThe installation check: the PHP runtime and its extensions, directory permissions, the database, the scheduler, updates, the MCP endpoint and the AI providers, each as a row with a status and a hint about what to do. This is the first thing to call when something is not working. It reads only: nothing here is changed. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Read the audit log reads adminRecent administrative actions - accounts created, roles changed, settings saved, connections revoked, updates installed - newest first, with who did it, when, from where, and whether it came through the web interface or through MCP. action matches the start of the action name, so "user" covers user.create, user.role and user.delete. The values of settings are never recorded here, only their keys. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description action string Keep only actions starting with this, for instance "user", "settings" or "update". limit integer How many entries to return. Defaults to 100.

List MCP connections reads adminEvery MCP connection on this installation: its name, the account it belongs to, the tool groups it is limited to, when it was made, when it was last used and how often. Tokens are stored only as hashes and can never be shown again. Use the connection_id from here with revoke_connection. Your own unless you name another account or ask for all of them. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description owner string One other account's connections. all boolean Administrators only: widen to every account on the installation. Without it a listing is your own.

Revoke an MCP connection writes destructive adminDeletes one connection's token, so the next request it makes is refused. Revoking the connection you are talking through ends this conversation immediately, and no further tool call will work - call list_connections first and be sure which one you have, and check the name against the one this conversation is using. This cannot be undone: a new connection has to be made from the Connect screen. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description connection_id * integer The connection to revoke, as returned by list_connections. confirm_name * string The exact name of that connection, as a confirmation that the right one is being cut off.

Check for a new version writes adminAsks GitHub whether a newer release exists and reports what is installed, what is available and whether the two differ. force ignores the cached answer and asks again, which is worth doing straight after a release and not much otherwise, because GitHub allows anonymous callers only sixty requests an hour per address. Nothing is downloaded or replaced here - install_update does that. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description force boolean Ignore the cached answer and ask GitHub again.

Update status reads adminWhat the updater knows: the installed version, when it last checked, whether an update is waiting, whether automatic updates are switched on, and which backups are on disk to roll back to. It answers from the cached check where it can and asks GitHub only when that cache has gone stale, so it is the cheap way to ask; check_for_update is the one that always goes out. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Install the update writes destructive adminDownloads the latest release and replaces the application's own files with it. A backup of the current version is taken first, so a version that fails to start can be put back with rollback_update. This takes minutes and rewrites the code that is answering you, so do not run it while a generation run is writing pages, and expect this call to be slow. Call check_for_update first to see what would be installed, because confirm_version has to name it exactly. Settings and data are never touched: they live outside the release directory. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description confirm_version * string The version that would be installed, exactly as check_for_update or get_update_status reports it under latest.version. The install is refused unless the two agree.

Roll an update back writes destructive adminPuts the previously installed version back from the backup the last update took. Use it when a new version does not start or breaks something. With no backup on disk there is nothing to restore and the call reports that rather than doing anything. get_update_status lists what backups exist. confirm has to be true, because this replaces the running application with an older one and anything the newer version wrote to the database stays as it is. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description confirm * boolean Must be true. Without it nothing is restored and the call reports what it would have done.

Read the update log reads adminEvery update and rollback this installation has attempted, newest first: which version it came from and went to, who asked for it, whether it was a manual or an automatic attempt, how it ended, the log it wrote and the error if it failed. This is where to look when a version is not the one somebody expected. Alongside it: the backups on disk and whether an update is running right now. Costs nothing. No arguments.

Read the prompt library reads adminThe prompt library: every instruction CourseForge sends a model, as a named slot you can read and rewrite. A slot is one piece of the eventual prompt - the persona the model writes as, the format contract an outline has to obey, the audience block, the tagging rules, the language instruction - and they are joined together for each job. Each slot comes back with its group, its label, what it is for, the placeholders it may use, the text this installation currently sends, the text the release ships, and whether the two differ. These are the installation-wide base layer: a profile may still override any slot for its own courses, and get_profile shows what a profile has changed. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description group string One group of slots only, as returned in groups. Omit for the whole library.

Rewrite the prompt library writes adminRewrites one or more prompt slots for the whole installation, which is how the house style of everything CourseForge writes gets tuned. prompts is an object of slot key to new text, and only the slots you name are touched. An empty string is not an empty prompt: it drops this installation's override and puts the shipped default back. An unknown slot key is refused and nothing is written. Keep the placeholders the slot declares - they are filled in at generation time and a slot that loses one silently loses the thing it named. Read get_prompts first for the keys, the current text and the defaults. This is the base layer only: a profile can still override any of these for its own courses. Costs nothing. Argument Type Description prompts * object Slot key to new text, for instance {"global_system": "You are a patient technical writer."}. An empty string resets that slot to the shipped default.

CourseForge has real accounts, stored in its database, with two roles: user and administrator. They are all managed from Administration › Accounts. Administration › Accounts: everybody who may sign in, and the invites still open.

A fresh installation has no accounts. Its setup screen asks for the code in INVITE-CODE.txt - a file CourseForge writes next to index.html, or into data/ when the install root is not writable - and creates the first administrator from it. See Installation for why that is enough. Only the hash is stored. The plain code exists in that file and nowhere else. It is spent on use. The file is deleted the moment the account is created. The door closes for good. Once any account exists, setup reports needs_setup: false and refuses to create anything. It can be taken back. Revoke beside the open invite closes it and deletes its file. On Apache the shipped .htaccess refuses every .txt file, so the code cannot be downloaded even while it sits in the document root. nginx, Caddy and IIS ignore .htaccess: on those, configure the server first (Security) or move the data directory out of the web root. If every administrator password is lost, recover from the database: delete the rows in users, and the setup screen and a fresh code come back.

There are two ways, and they differ in who ends up knowing the password: How it works Use it when Create an account You set a password, or leave it blank and CourseForge generates one. It is shown once, and the account must choose its own at first sign-in. You hand somebody an account face to face. Issue an invite A code shown once, with a label (who it is for), a role, an expiry (48 hours by default, 30 days at most) and a number of places. The holder creates their own account with it. You would rather not send a password over chat. Several invites can be open at once - up to twenty-five - each with its own Revoke. Revoking one closes it immediately, wherever the code has been sent, and leaves accounts already created with it and the other invites alone. An invite worth more than one account (Good for, up to fifty) lets a whole group in with one code; raise it only for a group you are expecting, because the code is worth that many accounts to whoever holds it. A password needs at least ten characters and is stored with PHP's password_hash(), rehashed on sign-in whenever PHP's default cost moves. A user name may hold letters, digits, spaces and . _ @ + -, starts with a letter or digit, and can never change. Sign-in is throttled per account and per address: five failures inside fifteen minutes lock that address out for fifteen minutes (all three numbers are under Settings › Security). A locked account stays reachable from the address its owner last signed in from, so wrong guesses from elsewhere cannot lock the owner out. A missing account costs a full hash comparison, so "n

A user An administrator Their own courses, profiles, tags, connections yes yes Everybody's courses no yes Accounts, invites, roles no yes Settings, the prompt library, the cron token no yes Diagnostics, the audit log, security, updates no yes The Administration group appears in the sidebar only for an administrator, and every route behind it is checked twice - by the router and inside the handler. A role is read from the database on every request rather than kept in the session or a token, so demoting, disabling or deleting somebody takes effect on their next request, including on MCP connections they already made.

Every course, profile, tag, connection and run belongs to the account that created it. Two questions are kept apart: May you reach this? - asked of you, the actor. Whose is it? - everything downstream uses the owner's data. So an administrator who opens somebody else's course works with that course's profile, tags and BookStack instance, never their own. Generating a page there spends the owner's AI account, and an administrator cannot lend their own API key to somebody else's course by assigning one of their profiles to it. A row you may not reach is reported as not found rather than forbidden: telling somebody that course 47 exists but is not theirs is a small leak that costs nothing to avoid.

Courses widens by itself to every account, each row marked with its owner, with a filter to narrow it back. A course list is an inventory, and that is what an administrator is for. Profiles, tags and connections stay the administrator's own in the browser - they are working sets, and somebody else's profile in your picker is a trap. Add ?owner=name for one other account, or ?all=1 for everybody. Over MCP, list_profiles and list_tags make the opposite choice for an administrator and return every account's rows, marked with their owner.

Deleting an account never silently deletes its courses. The dialog counts what the account owns and asks which you mean: transfer hands the courses, profiles, runs and connections to another account, and merges the tag library into theirs by name; delete removes all of it, cascading through chapters, pages, tag links and runs. Destroying anything asks for the user name to be typed first. Three things the server refuses whatever the browser sends: deleting or disabling the account you are signed in with, removing your own administrator rights, and deleting, disabling or demoting the last enabled administrator.

h: Handing one course to somebody else
t: What happens to it The course, its chapters and pages move The run history moves, so the course does not look never-generated to its new owner The tag links are re-pointed at the receiving library by name; missing tags are created The profile is cleared, not shared - it carries an API key. The new owner picks one of their own. The published book is untouched. Publishing again needs a profile with a BookStack instance of the same name. A tag that exists in the receiving library with a different value keeps the receiving value, so the pages carrying it go out of sync and the next push rewrites the tag. A course with a run in flight refuses to move: that run is billed to the old owner's account. There is no button for this in the browser. It is transfer_course over MCP, or POST api/projects/{id}/transfer, both for administrators.

One line per administrative act - an account created, a role changed, a setting saved, a connection issued or revoked, an invite revoked, a security risk accepted, an update installed or rolled back - with who, when, from which address, and whether it came from the web, MCP, cron or the command line. Five thousand entries are kept. Nothing secret is ever written to it: a setting change records the key, never the value.
list_users, create_user, update_user, delete_user, issue_invite (with label and max_uses), revoke_invite, transfer_course and get_audit_log, all in the admin group. See the MCP tool reference.

Administration › Settings holds everything the installation can be told to do differently, one card per group. There are 60 settings in 8 groups. Each field carries its own description, its range and whether this installation has changed it. Settings, one card per group. The scheduler card writes the cron line out for you.

text Copyconfig/defaults.json ships with the release: settings, the security policy, the content details and the whole prompt library. Replaced by every update. Never written to. data/config.json what this installation changed, and only that. Written from the admin screens. No update touches it. Splitting them is what makes an update safe: a new release brings new defaults and new prompt slots, and your decisions live in a file the update may not write. It also makes Reset a delete rather than a copy - setting a value back to the shipped default removes it from data/config.json, which stays a short, readable list of what this installation actually decided. Every setting is declared once in the code (Support\Settings). The Settings screen draws a field from that declaration, the API validates against it, and the MCP tools describe and change settings from it - so a setting added in a release appears in all three at once. The reference below is generated from the same declaration.

app.cron_token - the secret in the URL your host calls once a minute. Without one, cron.php answers 404 to everybody and CourseForge offers no background runs at all. At least sixteen characters; the screen generates one and hands you the finished URL. Rotating it invalidates the old URL immediately. See The scheduler. app.cron_workers - how many scheduler ticks may work side by side, which is where parallelism in background generation comes from. Raise it only as far as your provider's rate limits allow; too high gives a run full of 429 errors, not a faster course. The timeouts - app.ai_timeout_seconds defaults to 1800, because a long page on a reasoning model takes minutes; below about 600 you will lose work the provider was about to deliver. Your web server has its own limit too, and the smallest one wins. updates.auto_install - off by default. On, the installation replaces its own files unattended at the configured hour. It backs up first and rolls back if the new version fails to start, but it is still an unattended change to a production system. See Updates. mcp.allowed_origins - empty by default, which refuses every browser-based MCP client and affects nothing else. Add an exact origin only when you have such a client. app.debug - puts exception details and stack traces into API responses and MCP errors. Leave it off on anything reachable from the internet. app.task_max_attempts - how often a publish that ran into trouble is resumed before it is given up (twenty by default). Each attempt waits longer, up to a quarter of an hour. Two settings hold secrets - app.cron_t

The Settings screen also carries Diagnostics - the same rows php tools/diagnose.php prints: PHP version and extensions, writable directories, the database, the scheduler's last tick, open invites - and Set up PHP, which raises PHP limits that are too low through .user.ini (Installation).

list_settings, set_settings and reset_setting in the admin group reach every setting by its key, with the same validation as the screen. generate_cron_token rotates the cron token; get_cron_url reads the URL.

The cron endpoint that keeps writing courses after the browser is closed. Setting Default What it does Cron tokenapp.cron_token empty The secret in the URL your host calls once a minute. Without one, cron.php answers 404 to everybody and background runs are not offered at all. Seconds of work per tickapp.cron_seconds 50 A tick stops handing out new pages after this long, so it finishes before your host cuts the request off. Keep it under the PHP time limit. Range 5-3000 seconds. Parallel workersapp.cron_workers 2 How many ticks may work side by side. Two writes roughly two pages a minute. Raise it only as far as your provider rate limits allow. Range 1-16. Attempts per pageapp.cron_max_attempts 3 How often a page that fails is handed back to a later tick before it is given up on. Range 1-10. Worker leaseapp.cron_item_timeout_seconds 1800 How long a page stays claimed by a worker that has stopped answering, before another one may take it. Range 60-7200 seconds. Attempts per publishapp.task_max_attempts 20 How often a publish or a link pass that ran into trouble - a wiki that stopped answering, a host time limit - is picked up again from where it stopped before it is given up on. Each attempt waits a little longer than the last, up to a quarter of an hour, and a task that was given up on can still be retried by hand. Range 1-200.

How queued generation is polled and how long its records are kept. Setting Default What it does Minimum time between pollsapp.batch_poll_seconds 60 How rarely CourseForge asks a provider whether a queued batch has finished. Batches take hours; polling every minute wastes rate limit for nothing. Range 10-3600 seconds. Keep finished runs forapp.batch_keep_days 30 Finished run records are removed after this long. The pages they wrote are never touched. Range 1-3650 days. Default output ceilingapp.anthropic_max_tokens 32000 Used where a provider demands an explicit ceiling and the profile does not set one. Too low truncates a long page mid-sentence: a page at the shipped maximum length of 15,000 words is well over 20,000 tokens, which is why this ships at 32,000. A model whose own ceiling is lower is held to that ceiling, never to this number. Range 1000-200000 tokens.

Leave it empty and the server's own time zone is used, which is almost always the one you meant. GitHub tokenupdates.github_token empty Only needed for a private fork, or to lift the 60-requests-an-hour limit GitHub applies per IP address to anonymous callers.

Background runs, batch collection, publish tasks, the security re-check and unattended updates all need something to call CourseForge once a minute. Without it, CourseForge still works - but only while a browser tab is open. Without a scheduler With one Pages are written only by an open tab Background runs and batches, with the tab closed A push is worked by the open tab, one slice per request A push carries on with the laptop shut Batches are never collected Batches are polled and collected No unattended updates Daily update checks and optional installs

Open Administration › Settings › Scheduler and click Generate next to the cron token. The card shows the finished URL and the crontab line, with the token and the absolute path filled in. On a host with a control panel (all-inkl/KAS, Plesk, cPanel, DirectAdmin…), add a cron job that calls the URL every minute: text Copyhttps://your-install/cron.php?token=<your cron token> every minute The token can also be sent as an X-Cron-Token header, for a scheduler that supports headers. On a host with a real crontab, skip the web server and the token entirely: crontab Copy* * * * * php /path/to/courseforge/tools/cron.php --quiet Watch the card: it shows how long ago the last tick was. That number is the one to check - a scheduler configured six months ago that stopped calling last week looks exactly like one that was never set up. php tools/diagnose.php and the Scheduler row of Diagnostics say whether it is actually running.

In this order, and for a reason: gives back any page or task whose worker died (an expired lease); collects finished provider batches; works publish tasks, then writes pages, until its time is up; only then considers an unattended update - because an update replaces the very files the tick is running, everything still owed to a course is done first. The scheduler also re-takes the security check every six hours. Nothing is unbounded. A tick cut short by a host time limit loses nothing, because every claim is a lease with an expiry and every page is stored the moment it is finished.

app.cron_workers decides how many ticks may work side by side. With two, a tick that arrives while the previous one is still busy takes the second slot instead of waiting, and roughly twice as many pages get written per minute. A tick that finds every slot busy exits immediately, so calling once a minute is safe at any setting. Raise it only as far as your provider's rate limits allow. The other scheduler settings - how long a tick works, how often a failed page is retried, how long a worker's claim lasts, how many attempts a publish task gets - are listed on the Settings reference.

cron.php in the document root is meant to be reachable: it is the only thing a control-panel scheduler can call. It compares the token in constant time and answers 404 to everything else, including when no token is configured - so an installation that never set one has no open endpoint. Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed, because a token pasted into a control panel often arrives with one. Run from a shell, cron.php refuses and points at tools/cron.php, with a failing exit status - the likely reader is a crontab pointed at the wrong file, and a clean exit would let it report success every minute while nothing ticks. Rotating the token invalidates the old URL immediately: update the control panel in the same sitting.

CourseForge keeps everything in data/: the SQLite database with every password hash and, in plain text, every AI key and BookStack token the installation has been given. They are never sent back to a browser and never written to the audit log, but at rest they are readable by anyone who can read the file. So the one thing that must never be true is that data/app.sqlite can be fetched over HTTP. CourseForge protects itself with .htaccess files - and a file the server may not read is not a promise. So it checks.

The verdict, the server CourseForge detected, and the configuration to paste for it. The installation writes a small probe file into the data directory and fetches it - along with the database, the deny file, the shipped configuration, the invite file while there is one, and a few files that should not be served - from its own public address, reading a few kilobytes of each. The verdict: Verdict Means secure every file that holds a secret was refused. Keys and tokens may be stored. exposed at least one came back. Nothing that would store a secret is allowed to, and anything already stored should be treated as read. unverified the server could not reach itself: no public address is known (set app.public_url), or the host blocks requests to its own name. unknown nobody has checked yet. The check runs the first time the screen opens, then every six hours from the scheduler. Each file the check asked for, and what came back. Until the verdict is secure, every field that would store a secret is locked: API keys and BookStack tokens on profiles, the cron and GitHub tokens in Settings. They are greyed out with a red mark, an administrator sees a banner on every screen, and the API refuses the write whichever door it comes through, MCP included. Nothing already stored stops working. The screen names the server it detected - Apache, LiteSpeed, nginx, Caddy, IIS or PHP's own - with the configuration block to paste for it (switchable by hand, because a proxy can make the detection wrong), lists every file it asked for and what came back, and repeats the one arrangement that is safe on

At the bottom, framed in red, an administrator who has verified the server by hand - behind a proxy that will not let it fetch itself, say - can accept the risk by typing back a six-character code shown on the screen. The fields unlock, and the acceptance is written to the audit log with their name. It can be withdrawn, and the lock holds again.

h: The safest arrangement: data outside the web root
t: Point CourseForge at a data directory the web server does not serve, and the question of what refuses data/ stops arising: Apache CopySetEnv COURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR /var/lib/courseforge nginx Copyfastcgi_param COURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR /var/lib/courseforge; Then only index.html, assets/, api/, cron.php and bs.php need to be public. config/ must remain readable by PHP but not by the web.

h: Serving it somewhere other than Apache
t: nginx, Caddy, IIS and PHP's built-in server ignore .htaccess entirely. On those you reproduce the protection yourself. The shipped rules do five things: route /api/… to api/index.php, and /mcp to api/mcp.php; leave api/mcp.php alone - it is a second front door with its own authentication; deny all access to data/, config/, src/, tools/ and tests/; deny *.sqlite (and its -wal, -shm, -journal files), *.db, *.json, *.md, *.log, *.ini, *.txt, *.zip, *.tar, *.gz, *.bak, *.sql and *.sh everywhere; re-expose the Authorization header, which Apache drops under CGI/FastCGI - without it every MCP request looks unauthenticated. .php is deliberately not on the deny list, because the application is made of PHP files. Routing itself is optional - the app calls api/index.php?r=<route> and works with no rewrite rules at all - but the directory and file-type protection is not.

nginx Copy# Block the private directories outright location ^~ /data/ { deny all; return 403; } location ^~ /config/ { deny all; return 403; } location ^~ /src/ { deny all; return 403; } location ^~ /tools/ { deny all; return 403; } location ^~ /tests/ { deny all; return 403; } # Block sensitive file types anywhere. .txt is here for INVITE-CODE.txt. location ~* \.(sqlite|sqlite3|sqlite-wal|sqlite-shm|sqlite-journal|db|db-wal|db-shm|json|md|log|ini|txt|zip|tar|gz|bak|sql|sh)$ { deny all; return 403; } # API front controller.
