Use <requestFiltering><hiddenSegments> for the five directories and <fileExtensions> for the suffixes, in web.config. IIS does not read .htaccess and does not fall back to it, so nothing is protected until that file exists.

tools/router-dev.php reproduces the directory rules and the database suffixes for development, but not the .json, .txt or .md deny - under php -S, config/defaults.json and INVITE-CODE.txt can be downloaded. Fine on a laptop; not a way to serve anybody else.

The release ships data/.htaccess, which denies everything in that directory. Because there are ordinary ways to end up without it - PHP creating a missing directory empty, an update never writing into data/, a deploy tool that skips data/ - CourseForge writes the file itself, from a constant in the code, on the way to opening the database. A file already there is left alone, including one you edited. A missing data/.htaccess is therefore reported as a failure by the installation check: it can only mean PHP was refused permission to write it.

h: Hardening applied regardless of the server
t: Sessions: the cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, scoped to the install directory, and Secure whenever HTTPS is detected (including behind a proxy that sets X-Forwarded-Proto). Strict mode, so a made-up session id is never adopted; the id is renewed on sign-in and on a password change. Requests: every non-GET request needs a CSRF token; bodies above 16 MB are refused before they are read. Headers: every response sends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Cache-Control: no-store; on Apache also X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Referrer-Policy: same-origin and a Content-Security-Policy of frame-ancestors 'self'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'; form-action 'self'. A script-src is deliberately not sent: the import map is inline and changes every release, and Vue's runtime template compiler needs 'unsafe-eval'. Outbound addresses a profile carries are vetted before they are stored: http or https only, a host, no credentials in the address, never the cloud metadata range (a local model server on the same machine is allowed). What an address answers is never quoted back verbatim. The HTTP client speaks HTTP and HTTPS only and follows redirects only to HTTPS, only for BookStack. Secrets on profiles are kept only for the address they were stored against. Host headers: Host is used for the addresses CourseForge hands out only when it looks like a host, and X-Forwarded-Host never; behind a rewriting proxy set app.public_url and mcp.public_url. Throttling: sign-ins and password changes are throttled per account and per address, in the browser and over MCP. Rendering: previews are sanitise

data/ is the installation: app.sqlite and config.json. Back it up like the secret it is - a copy of the database holds every API key in plain text. The update backups under data/backups/ are single zip archives on purpose: a backup tree would be a runnable second copy of the application under data/.

CourseForge can replace itself with a newer release from GitHub: from Administration › Updates, from php tools/update.php --install, or unattended at a fixed hour. It is the most dangerous thing the application does - the files being replaced are the files doing the replacing - so every step is arranged around one rule: a failed update must leave the old version running.

A check reads the latest release from api.github.com (or the twenty most recent when the channel includes pre-releases) and caches the answer for an hour; a failed check backs off for fifteen minutes. Both windows exist because GitHub allows sixty unauthenticated requests an hour per address. Check now forces a fresh answer, and installing always asks afresh. A 403 from GitHub is usually the rate limit; the screen reports when it lifts. Set updates.github_token to raise the allowance, or to update from a private fork.

Every condition is checked separately, before anything is downloaded, so the answer is never just "the update failed": Check Blocking Why Updates are switched on yes updates.enabled off means CourseForge never contacts GitHub A repository is configured yes nowhere to fetch from otherwise PHP can open a zip archive yes, for zip releases ext-zip PHP may write to the installation yes it is about to rewrite the document root PHP may write to the data directory yes the download, staging and backup live there No update is already running yes one at a time, across every tab and worker A newer version is available yes reinstalling the same version is not an update No generation run is in flight warning pages are stored as they finish; a worker mid-request is retried later Room for the download and a backup warning about three times the release size php tools/update.php --status prints the same rows with OK, WARN or FAIL.

Download the release asset, or GitHub's zipball when there is none, straight to a file - never into memory. Only GitHub's own hosts are ever fetched from. Verify the SHA-256 digest if the release publishes one. A published digest that does not match is never allowed through; a missing one is allowed and logged. Extract into data/updates/, checking every entry name first - a zip may contain ../../etc/passwd. Confirm it is CourseForge by looking for src/bootstrap.php, config/defaults.json and api/index.php. Warm up: load every class the rest of the update needs while the old files are still on disk, so nothing from the new release is mixed into the running process. Back up, completely, before replacing anything: every file the swap will touch, plus a manifest, in one zip under data/backups/. Swap, file by file. The install root is never renamed wholesale - the web server is pointed at it, and the running script lives inside it. Prove it works, and roll back if it does not. data/ is never touched, whatever the archive contains, and neither are INVITE-CODE.txt, .git and .github.

A finished update has to prove itself: every installed PHP file is parsed - which catches a copy cut short by a full disk; the new config/defaults.json is read and the database is opened; the version is read back out of the installed src/bootstrap.php and must be newer than the old one; then a child process boots the new code from scratch, loads every class and opens the database - which runs the new release's migration - and reports the schema version it arrived at. The child process is the part that matters: the running process still holds the old classes and the old database handle, so only a fresh PHP can prove the new release starts and migrates. On hosts where PHP may not start programs (proc_open disabled, as on most shared hosting) that one check is skipped, and the log says so plainly: the database migration was NOT tested.

If the smoke check reports anything - or anything throws after the backup exists - the backup goes straight back, the configuration cache is flushed, and the history records rolled_back with the reason. If even the rollback fails, the log says where the archive is so it can be unpacked over the installation by hand. Rollback on the Updates screen, or php tools/update.php --rollback, restores the most recent backup on demand: files back, files the update added removed, and the file-level checks run again. updates.keep_backups decides how many backups are kept (two by default). Zero deletes the one just taken - and the log says the update cannot be rolled back. Every attempt is a row in the update history with its full log, and a line in the audit log.

updates.auto_check asks GitHub once a day, so the Updates screen is current when you open it. updates.auto_install installs at updates.auto_time in updates.timezone. Off by default. Both need the scheduler. A few deliberate details: "Once a day" means a calendar day, not a minute: a host that runs cron every five minutes, a tick that overran or a server asleep at the chosen hour still gets its update that day - late rather than not at all. A clock put back an hour cannot cause a second run. A busy installation gets two hours' grace. A run in flight defers the update; after two hours it goes ahead, because a run open all morning is more likely stuck than busy. The day's slot is spent before the install starts, so an update that crashes the process is not retried a minute later. One that was refused - a failed precondition - gives the slot back.

tools/update.php does the same work without a browser tab that can be closed half way: bash Copyphp tools/update.php --status # what is installed, what is available, preconditions php tools/update.php --check # ask GitHub now, ignoring the cache php tools/update.php --install # install the newest release on the channel php tools/update.php --rollback # restore the most recent backup Nothing is interactive. Add --quiet to print only what went wrong. It is also the way in when the web application has stopped answering.
check_for_update, get_update_status, install_update, rollback_update and get_update_history, in the admin group.
Every release migrates its own database on first start, guarded by a schema version, and never touches a value you have since edited. Take a copy of data/ before a major upgrade anyway.

Use Administration › Updates or php tools/update.php --install. See Updates. 5.2 → 5.3: the database gains one column (pages.scope). Existing courses have no page scopes until the outline is revised or Plan missing scopes is pressed on the Structure tab; until then they are written as before, with the compact course map. Claude is now asked on API version 2026-10-21, so the profile's temperature no longer applies to Claude models. 5.1 → 5.2: publishing became a background task. Set up the scheduler if you have not, or keep the Publish tab open while a push runs. → 5.1: the Claude subscription AI account type was retired. A profile that still has one keeps it, marked as retired; point it at an API provider, or connect the Claude app over MCP instead.

Nothing to do, and nothing is republished. Schema 8 moved each course's single destination into the destination list: one row with the same instance, shelf, book and fingerprint, and one record per chapter and page that had been published. The old columns are still written as a mirror of the first destination, so a rollback to 4.6 finds its first book intact; what a rollback loses is any second destination.

Copy your data/ directory across, or point the new installation at the old one with COURSEFORGE_DATA_DIR. Three things happen on first start, each exactly once: the database gains its new tables (users, invites, audit_log, update_history, locks, and more) and columns; data/users.json is imported as administrator accounts and renamed to users.json.imported; data/config.json is reduced to the settings you actually changed, so the new defaults apply to everything else. AI accounts with no type recorded are read as the OpenAI-compatible accounts they were. Connection tokens issued by CourseForge 3 (cf3_…) stay valid until revoked. Warningconfig/ is new since 4.0. A deployment that copies only the files it recognises will leave config/defaults.json behind, and nothing starts: the API answers "the server is not configured correctly" and the real message goes to the server log. php tools/diagnose.php names it outright.

Point data/ at your existing installation's data directory, or copy app.sqlite, users.json and config.json across. CourseForge adds the new columns and converts the old per-level anki flag into the content-detail system. Projects, chapters, pages, tags, tag links and profiles - including stored secrets and prompt overrides - carry over untouched; anything the 2.x catalogue did not know about falls back to the defaults.
Open Administration › Security and check the verdict is still secure. Open Settings › Diagnostics and check the scheduler is ticking. Read the changelog for what changed in behaviour.
Start with the two built-in checks: Administration › Settings › Diagnostics (or php tools/diagnose.php from a shell) and Administration › Security. Between them they name most problems outright.

Almost always PHP older than 8.1: the interpreter cannot parse the code and serves nothing. Check the PHP version your host runs for this directory - control panels often default an old site to an old PHP.
config/defaults.json is missing - typically a deployment that copied only the files it recognised. Copy the whole release. The server log and php tools/diagnose.php name the path it expected.

h: The setup screen says it cannot write the invite code
t: Neither the install root nor data/ is writable by PHP. Make data/ writable by the PHP user and reload. The setup screen names the path it tried.

h: I lost the invite code before using it
t: Delete the open row from the invites table in data/app.sqlite and reload: a fresh code is written. If you already have an administrator, Revoke the invite on Administration › Accounts and issue a new one.

Delete the rows in the users table. The setup screen and a fresh invite code come back. Courses and profiles stay, owned by the old user names; create the new administrator with the same user name to keep them, or transfer them afterwards.

h: The API key fields are greyed out with a red mark
t: The security check has not passed, so CourseForge refuses to store secrets. Open Administration › Security: on Apache with the shipped .htaccess it usually passes by pressing Check again; on nginx, Caddy or IIS paste the configuration block the screen shows. See Security.

The server could not fetch its own address. Set Settings › General › Public address (app.public_url) if CourseForge guessed it wrong (behind a reverse proxy, for instance). Some hosts block requests to their own name; then verify the protection by hand and accept the risk at the bottom of the Security screen.
At least one private file can be downloaded. Fix the server configuration first, then treat every key already stored as compromised and rotate it at the provider.

h: Generation stops half way, or pages fail with a timeout
t: The smallest time limit between CourseForge and the model wins: app.ai_timeout_seconds (default 1800) - keep it above 600; PHP's max_execution_time and default_socket_timeout - Set up PHP raises them where the host allows; the web server: nginx fastcgi_read_timeout, a proxy timeout, a hosting-panel limit. Background runs are more robust than the in-tab generator here, because each page is its own short-lived request and is stored the moment it finishes.

h: A page failed with "cut off by the output limit"
t: The model hit the slot's token ceiling, and CourseForge refused to store a page that stops mid-sentence. Raise the page slot's token ceiling (or set it to 0 for the provider's maximum), or lower the course's maximum length.

Check the Structure tab for pages without a scope and press Plan missing scopes. Scopes are how a page knows what its neighbours own. Writing live in chapter order also helps: later pages see the headings of the pages already written in their chapter. See Tokens and caching.

h: A page ignores something I told it
t: Put page-specific facts in the inspector's context tab, which outranks the model's own assumptions. For a course-wide rule, use a profile prompt override or the course's content details. A rewrite with feedback corrects one written page.

h: The model refuses temperature, or the setting has no effect
t: Claude (API version 2026-10-21) and OpenAI's reasoning models refuse sampling parameters; CourseForge leaves them out, so the temperature has no effect on those models. That is expected.
Too many requests at once for your provider tier. Lower Pages in parallel on the profile for in-tab generation, or app.cron_workers for background runs. A batch run avoids rate limits altogether.

h: Pages from a local model ignore the course map or lose the thread
t: Ollama's OpenAI endpoint cannot set the context length, so long prompts are silently truncated. Raise OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH on the Ollama machine. Other local servers have a similar context setting.

Google is migrating Gemini API keys, and some new AQ. keys are refused by generateContent. CourseForge shows Google's own error verbatim; try a key of the other type, or use Gemini through OpenRouter. See AI providers.

h: The Content tab does not offer a background run
t: The scheduler is not set up or has never called in. Generate a cron token on Settings › Scheduler and add the URL to your host's cron, every minute. See The scheduler.

h: The scheduler says it has never run
t: Control-panel cron: check the URL and the token exactly (a trailing space is fine; a truncated token is not). cron.php answers 404 to a wrong or missing token. Crontab: point it at tools/cron.php, not cron.php. The web endpoint refuses to run from a shell.

The account cannot queue, and the reason is shown under the switch: the provider has no OpenAI-shaped queue (Mistral, local servers), the probe found none for this key, the key is on a free tier (Gemini's queue is paid-only), or the provider's queue does not accept the chosen model. Check this account re-probes.

h: A stopped batch run stays open
t: Cancelling a batch is asynchronous: the provider keeps what it finished, and the run closes once the provider confirms and the finished pages are collected. OpenRouter has no cancel route at all - its pages arrive when the provider is done. Check the run polls immediately.

h: A Gemini batch came back with nothing
t: Gemini expires a batch that is still running after 48 hours, with no results at all, not even partial ones. Submit the remaining pages again; smaller runs finish sooner.

The destination was removed and added again, or pointed at a different instance: CourseForge forgot the book it made there. To pause a destination, use its switch instead of removing it. Delete the duplicate book in BookStack.

h: Somebody edited a page in BookStack and CourseForge does not notice
t: CourseForge compares against what it last pushed, not against BookStack. Force overwrite re-sends every page and restores CourseForge's version. Edit in CourseForge rather than in the wiki.

h: A push keeps failing on one wiki
t: Read that destination's card and the publish log: the wiki's own error message is quoted. The other destinations carry on; the failed one is retried with growing pauses and can be retried by hand once fixed.

h: Code, diagrams and formulas show raw in BookStack
t: BookStack needs help to render them: give the wiki a BookStackDev look and paste its line into Settings › Customization › Custom HTML head content. If the loader is refused with a 403 in the browser console, add the wiki's origin to the look's allowed wikis.

h: Cross references stay as plain text
t: The target was not published yet (it resolves on the next publish), does not exist under that title, or the marker is inside code. The publish log reports markers that could not be matched. See Auto links.

h: Every MCP request is 401 on Apache
t: Apache drops the Authorization header under CGI/FastCGI. The shipped .htaccess re-exposes it - make sure it is deployed and AllowOverride permits it - or use the ?token= form of the URL.

h: The Claude desktop app cannot add the connector
t: Custom connectors are reached from the public internet, so localhost or a VPN-only address does not work. Use a public hostname or a tunnel, or configure the server in claude_desktop_config.json, which runs on your machine. See Connect an AI client.

h: Tool calls time out while a page is being written
t: Raise the client's tool timeout (Codex: tool_timeout_sec = 1800) and the server's own limits. Writing pages in the client with get_page_brief / write_page avoids long server calls altogether.

That is GitHub's rate limit of sixty unauthenticated requests an hour per address, usually shared with other sites on the host. The screen says when it lifts; set updates.github_token to raise the limit.

Read the log on Administration › Updates - it says which check failed. The previous version is running again, untouched. Common causes: PHP may not write to some files (a deploy that runs as a different user), or a disk filled up during the copy.

h: After an update some screens look old
t: The browser is holding a stale index.html. CourseForge serves it no-cache and stamps every asset with the release, so a normal reload fixes it; if a proxy cached it, a hard reload does.

h: Diagrams do not render in the preview on Safari
t: Mermaid 12 needs Safari 17.4 or later. The rest of the application works from Safari 16.4.

h: I am locked out after failed sign-ins
t: Five failures in fifteen minutes lock that address for fifteen minutes. Wait, or sign in from the address you last signed in from, which stays reachable.

CourseForge is a buildless single-page application plus a thin PHP JSON API, a second front door that speaks JSON-RPC for MCP clients, a scheduler endpoint and an endpoint that serves BookStackDev looks. There is no bundler, no package manager and no framework build step in any of them. Four front doors, one code base. Every door calls the same domain classes and the same access checks.

text Copyindex.html the import map and seven stylesheets assets/css/ tokens → base → layout → components → admin → prose → editor assets/js/ main → App → core/ + components/ + views/ + views/admin/ assets/vendor/ Vue, marked, DOMPurify, Fuse, CodeMirror, Shiki, Mermaid, MathJax (pinned; see VENDOR.md) assets/bookstackdev/ the BookStackDev files, as a wiki receives them config/defaults.json shipped settings, content-detail catalogue, prompt library data/ config.json (overrides only), app.sqlite, backups/, updates/ api/index.php the browser's front controller: every route, in one list api/mcp.php the MCP front door: bearer token, no cookie session cron.php the scheduler over HTTP, for hosts without a crontab bs.php BookStackDev looks, to the wikis that may load them src/Support/ Config, Settings, Db, Http, Request, Response, Router, Runtime, Audit, … src/Security/ Actor, Access, Auth, Users, Invite, Session, LoginThrottle, Hardening src/Domain/ Projects, Chapters, Pages, Tags, Profiles, Details, Structure, AutoLinker, LinkIndex, Runs, Targets, Tasks, Transfers, BookStackDev, … src/Ai/ Completion, AiRequest, CourseContext, PageGenerator, StructureGenerator, ScopePlanner, Research src/Ai/Provider/ one adapter each for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter and the OpenAI-compatible catch-all, plus Presets and Probe src/Ai/Batch/ the queue drivers (Anthropic inline, OpenAI file, Gemini LRO, OpenRouter inline) and the JSONL chunker src/Ai/Run/ RunManager, BatchDriver, LiveDriver src/Mcp/ Server (both protocol eras), Tools, Tool, Scopes, Resolve, Args, Prompts src/Mcp/Handlers/ one

Dependencies are vendored ES modules reached through bare specifiers in an import map, so application code reads import { ref } from 'vue' exactly as in a bundled project while deployment stays a file copy. The @/ prefix gives every module an absolute path to any other. Every asset URL carries the release (?v=5.3.0). With no build step nothing is ever renamed when its contents change, while the caching rules promise immutable for a year - so the version stamp is what makes an upgrade reach returning visitors. php tools/assets.php writes the stamp into index.html after CF_VERSION is bumped, and --check says whether it was forgotten. Every module is listed in the map individually (a prefix mapping cannot carry a query string), and no module imports another by a relative path (a query string is not inherited). index.html is the one file served no-cache. State is one reactive state object in core/store.js plus a few derived selectors: anything two views need lives in the store, anything one view needs stays in that view. All server traffic goes through core/api.js, which attaches the CSRF token, replays a request once after a 419, and turns an error envelope into an ApiError. Styling is a hand-written design system: tokens.css defines every colour, radius, shadow and type step for both themes, and nothing else hard-codes a colour. Templates are string templates compiled at runtime, which is why the full Vue build is vendored.

None of the four heavy libraries is on the critical path. CodeMirror arrives with the first tab that needs it; Shiki fetches one grammar per language actually shown, out of 232; Mermaid (vendored as its ES build with chunks, about 860 KB for a flowchart instead of a 5.5 MB single file) and MathJax load with the first diagram or formula. core/markdown.js renders Markdown synchronously and leaves a placeholder for each thing that needs a library - a cf-diagram div, a cf-code block, a cf-math span - which core/enhance.js fills in afterwards. Formulas are lifted out during tokenising, before CommonMark can mangle \( and x_i; sources travel as element text rather than attributes, because DOMPurify drops attribute values containing --> or <, which is what Mermaid arrows and LaTeX comparisons are made of. Everything is sanitised, Shiki's and Mermaid's output included. The split view is anchored on data-src-line, set on every top-level block; core/scrollsync.js interpolates between those anchors, with exactly one pane driving at a time. core/languages.js holds the language tables both halves share without either importing the other's library, and core/detect.js is the evidence-based language detector.

Everything a browser sends enters through api/index.php, which turns PHP warnings into exceptions (deprecations are logged, not thrown), guarantees a JSON body even when boot fails, enforces CSRF on non-GET requests and declares the whole HTTP surface as one list of routes - reading that file top to bottom gives you the entire API. Router matches path segments and answers 405 with an Allow header for a wrong verb. Request parses the body once and validates on demand; anything that is not an HttpException is logged and masked. Runtime::beginLongRequest() is what makes concurrent generation work: before any slow AI or BookStack call it closes the session (releasing PHP's session lock), lifts the time limit and sets ignore_user_abort, so requests of the same user do not queue behind each other and a closed tab does not discard a finished page.

Actor - who is asking: user name, display name, role, and the WHERE fragment every scoped query uses. Access - "may you reach this?": takes the actor and an id, returns the row, from which the caller reads the owner and carries on. A row you may not reach is reported as missing. Auth - the session holds a user name and nothing else that matters; role and existence are re-read on every request. The rule: authorisation reads the actor, data access reads the row's owner, and nothing outside src/Security/ consults the session.

Server is the transport and knows nothing about courses: era detection, version negotiation, the Origin check, the bearer token, the two response shapes. Tools is the registry and Tool one tool - definition and implementation in the same object, so they cannot drift. Resolve holds the two lines every handler starts with - authorise against the actor, then use the row's owner - and the handlers call the same domain classes as the HTTP controllers.

The Provider interface promises that chat() throws on any failure, including the ones that arrive as HTTP 200. AiRequest carries the system text, the shared context segments and the messages; each adapter maps the segments onto its provider's cache mechanism. Capability decisions come from the provider's model metadata where it exists (Anthropic) and from model-id rules where it does not (OpenAI), with a one-time retry on a 400 that blames a parameter.

TargetPublisher is idempotent by construction: every item is created once and updated afterwards, an item whose fingerprint matches what was last pushed to that wiki is skipped, and only a genuine 404 counts as "gone". Publisher fans out over destinations and folds their logs and counts into one answer. Since 5.2 a push is a row in Domain\Tasks, claimed under a lease and worked one tick's budget at a time; the publisher hands back its position (phase, last chapter and page, the link pass's cursor) so the next slice continues exactly there.

Everything lives in data/app.sqlite (WAL mode, foreign keys on): users, invites, profiles, projects, chapters, pages, tags and tag links, publish targets and items, runs (batch_jobs, batch_items), tasks and their log, leases, MCP clients, the audit log, update history, and a meta table for the schema version and installation facts. Content details are a JSON column per level, which is why the catalogue grows without migrations. The schema migrates itself on first open (schema version 11 in 5.3). Secrets: passwords as password_hash() digests, invite codes and connection tokens as SHA-256 (connection tokens are 32 random bytes and must be looked up by value, which a salted hash cannot do). Provider keys are stored so they can be sent, which is why profiles are redacted on the way out.

Title-based content preservation. Content is matched to the outline by title, so a revision keeps what was written. Prompt transparency. Every instruction is a documented, editable slot. Store the source, derive the output. Links are resolved on the way out; the stored text stays what was written. Declare it once. Settings, tools and the content-detail catalogue each exist in one place that every screen, endpoint and tool reads. Authorise against the actor, read against the owner. Resilience over speed. Long work survives a closed browser; an unparsable AI answer is refused rather than allowed to destroy existing work; an update that cannot prove it works is put back.

No framework, no dependencies - CourseForge installs without Composer, so its tests must run without it too. bash Copyphp tests/run.php # every test (434 in 5.3) php tests/run.php openrouter # only the files whose name contains that word node tools/outline-test.mjs # the JavaScript outline parser against the PHP one's fixtures node tools/detect-test.mjs # the language detector's corpus php tools/assets.php --check # every asset URL carries the current version The runner uses a scratch database in the system temp directory, never data/. The files worth reading first are the ones whose failure mode is silent: adapters.test.php (failures at HTTP 200), access.test.php (actor versus owner), tasks.test.php (resumable publishing), jsonl-chunker.test.php, typography.test.php and course-context.test.php (page scopes and cache-ordered prompts).

Bump CF_VERSION in src/bootstrap.php and run php tools/assets.php to restamp index.html. Add a "What is new in X.Y" section to README.md - it becomes the release notes and the changelog page. Tag vX.Y.Z and publish a GitHub release. Installations find it through Administration › Updates.

The documentation is generated from docs/pages/*.md by docs/build.mjs, which needs Node and PHP and nothing else: Markdown through the vendored marked, code highlighted at build time by the vendored Shiki, and the reference pages (MCP tools, settings, prompt slots, presets, content details) from php tools/docs-data.php, which reads the declarations in the code. bash Copynode docs/build.mjs # writes docs/dist/ php -S 127.0.0.1:8000 -t docs/dist # preview it with any static file server node docs/publish.mjs # build, then push docs/dist to the gh-pages branch GitHub Pages serves the gh-pages branch, which holds the generated site as a single commit replaced on every publish. A GitHub Actions workflow runs docs/publish.mjs on every push to main that touches the docs or the declarations they are generated from. The build fails on a link to a page or an anchor that does not exist.
Every installation offers new releases on Administration › Updates; see Updates and, for older versions, Upgrading. Downloads are on GitHub Releases.

Every page knows what every other page teaches. A push interrupted half way - a wiki that stopped answering, a host time limit, a process that died - is picked up again from the page it stopped at, never from the start, with a growing pause between attempts and a ceiling you can set. Eleven readers went over the whole application with one instruction — find what is actually wrong, not what could be tidier — and this release is what they found. Twenty-odd fixes and no features; the ones worth knowing about are below, in the order of the damage they did. Stopping a batch threw away the pages it had already written# "Stop this run" on a batch asked the provider to cancel and then closed the run on the spot: every page still waiting was released, and the run was over. But a cancel is asynchronous everywhere, and a batch keeps whatever it answered before the request landed — pages that were paid for. Nothing could download them while the batch was still winding down, and nothing ever tried afterwards, because a closed run is never polled. So the button reliably discarded finished work, and on OpenRouter — which has no cancel route at all — it closed the run while the batch ran on, billing, with nobody left to collect it. The run now stays open until the provider has said its last word. The next check collects the pages that were finished, releases only the ones that never ran, and closes the run then. A provider that cannot be stopped says so, and its run stays open for the same reason. A book created twice, once per retry# A course's first publish created its book, attached it to the shelf, and then wrote the book's id down. A shelf that had been deleted, or a token not allowed to edit shelves, failed the middle step — and the id was thrown away with the exception. The next push found no book on record, created another, and failed the same way: one orphaned

Two page counts disagreed, and the wrong one was believed# list_pages reported seven finished pages of a course as 194, 283 and 954 words long. They were 3,893, 4,677 and more. Nothing was lost — the count was wrong, and it was wrong in the direction that gets work destroyed: a model reading that list sees pages that look like failed generations and rewrites them, spending money to replace text that was already there. The count ran the Markdown through strip_tags first. Markdown is not HTML: List<String>, Map<String, Object> and a written-out <div class="card"> are prose about code, and strip_tags removes each of them along with everything up to the next >. Worse, a single a<b with no later > anywhere on the page is an unterminated tag, so the rest of the document is discarded — a 2,408-word page came back as two words. It now counts the page as it is stored, which is what get_page and the browser have always counted. Three surfaces answering "how long is this page" differently is worse than any one of them being wrong, because the difference reads as information. Everything the browser can do, a connected client can do# That was the claim. It was audited screen by screen against the tool registry, and it was untrue in eighteen places, so this release closes them. Thirteen new tools, and arguments added to five that existed. The punctuation pass reads a quotation mark the way a reader does# 4.6 taught CourseForge to set a generated page's punctuation the way its language sets it. It read each mark by position — a mark after a space opens, a mark after a word closes — and position turned out not to be enough twice over. **"Wort"** came out as **"Wort“**, because a Markdown asterisk stood where a space should have been and the opening rule declined the mark on its account. And correct French came out wrong: in « bonjour » et, the closing guillemet has a space on both sides, exactly like an opening one, so every » was turned back into a « — on text that had been right before the pass ran. The mark is now decided by three signals in order. Position first, with Markdown emphasis stepped over on the way to it, so a quotation with asterisks around it is still a quotation. Nesting depth second, which is what tells a closing guillemet from an opening one when both of its neighbours are spaces. The glyph last, for a mark that only ever points one way. And what gets written is not what was read: a closing mark takes the pair its own opening mark took, which is why „Wort" comes out as a pair at all, and why a double quotation inside a double quotation comes out as „… ‚…‘ …“ whichever character the model typed. The depth is forgotten at every blank line, heading, list item and table row, so one unbalanced mark costs its own paragraph instead of every paragraph after it. The rest of the pass grew with it, and all of it is code rather than a prompt — nothing here calls a model, and none of it costs anything:

A course can be published into more than one BookStack# A course used to have one destination. Choosing a second one meant a second course: the same outline, the same brief, the same pages generated and paid for twice, and two things to keep in step by hand for the rest of their lives. Course → Publish → Destinations is now a list. Add as many BookStack instances as the course's profile defines — a staging wiki and a live one, the wikis of two departments, a customer's install and your own — each with its own shelf. Publish everything goes to all of them; each one also has a button of its own, for the wiki that was behind. A destination has a switch: off keeps everything already published there on record and leaves it out of the next push, which is the difference between pausing a destination and removing one. Each destination holds its own book, and that is not a detail: the books have different ids and different slugs, and a page's cross references point inside the wiki it is in, so the same page is written slightly differently into each. A push knows what it last sent to each wiki separately, so the wiki that was already current is skipped there and rewritten here, and nothing is ever duplicated anywhere. A wiki that is down does not stop the others — its failure is named in the log, the rest still go out, and only a push where every destination failed is an error. The counts fold across the destinations that are on, which is what makes them worth reading: published means published in every one of them, out of sync means at least one would be written to. Punctuation set the way the language sets it# A model writing German opens a quotation with „ and closes it with a straight ". The two are one keystroke apart in the training data, it is not wrong enough to notice while reading one page, and it is wrong on every page of a five-hundred-page book — exactly the kind of error worth fixing with code rather than with a sentence in a prompt, because a rule that runs beats a rule that is asked for. A generated page now has its punctuation set before it is stored: German gets „Wort“, French its guillemets and the narrow spaces its typography asks for, Spanish and Italian their own guillemets, English its curly marks and a real apostrophe in don't. Every language gets ... as one character and a spaced hyphen as a dash. It never touches anything that is not prose. Fenced blocks, inline spans, links and their targets, bare addresses, HTML tags, formulas, a table's alignment row and CourseForge's own cross-reference and cloze markers are lifted out before the rules run and put back exactly as they were — a straight quote turned curly inside a JSON sample is not a typographic improvement, it is a broken example, and a course about a programming language is mostly examples. It reads position rather than order, which is what makes the half-corrected pair the models actually produce come out right. And it is idempotent, so a page written, regenerated and re-imported is byte-for-byte the page written once. Install the plugin" on the way out and read it back correctly — but only for outlines CourseForge had written itself. An outline written freehand, which is what a model or an MCP client produces, had nothing escaping it, and the length ceiling that was meant to be the net only caught paragraphs over 200 characters. Research the subject once, before the course is designed# A course about WordPress, a framework, an API or a standard is out of date the moment the model's training data is. The facts are established once, stored on the course with the date they were established, and read from then on by the outline and by every single page.
